# AxiomDynamics — Current State

**Last updated:** 2026-11-10 (chat-4 closed — ledger replication series built and
twice audited, the A1/D08 model decision taken and both documents plus `roi.py`
restated, the A1 workbook rebuilt). Next session: read
`chat-5/CARRY-FORWARD.md`, then this file.
**Repository:** `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics`
**Remote:** `github.com/kaanju19-lang/AxiomDynamics` (private)
**Push state:** `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` is the only answer that
counts. As last confirmed the local remote-tracking ref stood at `bb99cdd`; the
first commit after it is `893096e`. Never trust a hash written in this file
— check with git, because this file's own commit moves the top of the branch
every time it is edited. Run `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the repo root. The sandbox
cannot reach GitHub: `git push` and `git fetch` both fail with HTTP 403 from the
proxy, so a local `origin/main` ref is not proof of what the remote holds.

---

## What this project is

Physics-first predictive maintenance for freight rail. Six named physical models
— thermodynamics with per-axle rolling z-score, peer median/MAD comparison,
kinematics, acoustics (BPFO/BPFI/BSF/FTF), same-axle left/right differential, and
an executive ROI panel — instead of black-box ML or fixed alarm thresholds.

The Master Brief Docket is in `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/`: 38 artifacts
— 36 Markdown documents, the A1 Excel model (with its build script beside it) and
the B03 HTML infographic — across A (commercial), B (technical), C (deployment)
and D (contractual) series plus F (forms).

## Build status

**38 artifacts on disk; 37 docket IDs on disk (A1 is a folder holding the `.xlsx`
and the builder, so it counts as one ID and two files).** The docket index (D00)
carries 37 ID rows; 34 are marked `**Built**` in bold, and B02 (.md) and B03
(.html) carry plain "Built" with a format qualifier. D00 Part IV is the authority
on status, not this file.

A long-form account of the whole build — every stage, every document, every
correction, and the loss and rebuild — is at
`project-logs/AxiomDynamics-Build-History-and-Working-Summary.docx` (32 pages,
revised 2026-11-10 to carry Stages 6 and 7). It is generated by
`project-logs/build-history-summary.js`; re-run
`node project-logs/build-history-summary.js` after a material change.

Open docket items are tracked in **D00 Part IV** — that table is the authority,
not this file.

## The largest known gap

**There is no detector ingest path.** No endpoint accepts a Railroad payload.
Every demonstration signal is generated from the physics equations on synthetic
traces. This is disclosed in B01 §7 gap #5, B02 §2 and the B03 status block.

Every demonstration number demonstrates **the method**, not the Railroad's data.
The validation chain — schema, timestamp, plausibility — is designed and not built.

## Open items, in priority order

1. **D07 §14.5 — governing law and venue.** An open counsel decision, correctly
   labelled as open as of chat-2 (previously a blank pointing at an Order field
   that does not exist). Must be closed by signed addendum before first execution.
2. **Ledger signer attribution and off-box carriage** — the signed export landed
   2026-11-09 and the **series build landed 2026-11-10**, so the Platform now
   produces the D09 §4.5.4 cadence itself. What remains: the HMAC signature is
   symmetric, so it cannot name the signer; it cannot prove when it was made; a
   ledger wiped before the first bundle in a series is invisible to later ones;
   and **nothing carries the produced series off the box** — that is deliberate,
   because D09 §3.2 promises no outbound network, so carriage is the Railroad's
   physical step under §3.3. D09 §4.4–4.5, B01 §4.5a and §7 items 11–12.
   Closing attribution is an **AD-2 dependency**, not more export code.
3. **D09 §4.4 supply-chain gaps** — SBOM (Q1 2027), hash verification of
   dependency downloads (Q1 2027), GPG-signed releases (Q2 2027). All disclosed.

## Model decision — A1 governs, decided 2026-11-10 (chat-4)

The owner delegated the choice ("you decide"). **A1 governs the commercial
numbers, expressed as Option D in `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md`**:
0.05% escalation probability, $500,000 typical contained cost, $1.0B catastrophic.

What changed in the docket, all on 2026-11-10:

- **A2 §3.2 and D08 §3** anchors restated from the withdrawn 2.0x/4.1x to
  **1.77x at 500 axles, 3.36x at 10,000**, with the cost basis stated in the text
  instead of left to inference. The pilot year is charged in full and credited with
  no benefit in that calculation — the conservative frame.
- **D08 §5 restated** from A1: pilot year at the **200 axles §2 actually scopes**
  ($278,670 modelled benefit, **0.75x** the $370,000 fee — the pilot does not pay
  for itself and the document now says so); production years at 500 axles
  ($696,675/yr); four-year return **2.01x**.
- **D08 §6 restated**: six-year return **2.06x**. Close to flat against the
  four-year figure, because fee escalation from Year 4 offsets the dilution of one
  weak pilot year across more production years. It does **not** fall.
- **`backend/roi.py`** corrected: `P_CATASTROPHIC_GIVEN_MISSED_DEFECT` 2% → 0.05%,
  and the per-missed-defect value now blends the **$500,000 typical** cost rather
  than the $9.25M midpoint of the two NTSB severe benchmarks. Expected cost per
  missed defect is now **$999,750**, identical to A1's B22; the 29x overstatement is
  gone. The severe benchmarks survive as `SEVERE_FAILURE_COST_*`, explicitly
  reference-only, and the dataclass field renamed `severe_cost_range_usd` so no
  reader mistakes them for the typical case again.
- Checkers updated rather than left certifying stale text: the arithmetic pass is
  now **89 checks** and reports both findings **closed and checked**, not merely
  recorded. The decision paper's **65 checks** still reproduce (it documents the
  withdrawn figures, which is its job).

**Two things a future reader will otherwise trip over.** First, A2 §3.2 says 1.77x
at 500 axles and D08 §5 says 2.01x — different questions on the same inputs (A2
charges the pilot with no benefit; D08 credits the 200-axle pilot with its actual
benefit). A2 §3.2 now states that difference explicitly. Second, **D08 §2 scopes the
pilot at 100–200 axles**, so any pilot-year benefit computed at 500 was contradicting
the document's own scope. That defect was mine, introduced in the first restatement
and caught before commit.

## Ledger replication series — built 2026-11-10 (chat-4)

`backend/ledger_replication.py` executes the cadence D09 §4.5.4 already
specified: monthly full, weekly incremental, every bundle chained to the
previous by `previous_export_hash`, zero-record weeks kept, nothing overwritten.
`inspect` opens every bundle, recomputes its digest, verifies it against the
predecessor, and reports a missing period. 32 tests; full suite **112**.

**It deliberately does not transmit.** D09 §3.2 promises the Platform has no
outbound network, so the series accumulates in `--series-dir` on the box and
carrying it to backup media is the Railroad's step under §3.3. The owner chose
this over a network push on 2026-11-10; the reasoning is in
`assets/ledger-replication-build-2026-11-10.md`.

**Two audits found nine material defects before this was called built** — the
count is in the assets file rather than here, but the shape is worth carrying:
the release verifier rejected every full export, `inspect` could not see
tampering or gaps, the period walker hung on a 53-week ISO year, concurrent runs
duplicated bundles, and one test passed only because the check it guarded was
absent. A green suite of 108 preceded all of it.

## Export hardened at chat-4's validation pass, 2026-11-10

Found by attacking the artifact rather than re-reading it, when the owner asked
for the completed work to be validated: **a written bundle accepted any extra
top-level field and both verifiers still returned `ok=True`.** The signature
covers a selected tuple and the digest names its fields, so a key added beside
them was unsigned — changeable after signing, and readable by a recipient as
though the bundle attested it.

Both `backend/ledger_export.py` and `tools/verify_ledger_export.py` now reject a
bundle whose top level is not exactly `format` / `manifest` / `records` /
`signature`, with the check named `bundle_no_extras`. The signing construction is
unchanged: a named field list is the correct way to sign, because it puts the
covered set in code rather than in the document. The gap was the absence of a
check on what else the document contains. One test added and mutation-tested in
both files; suite 113 → **114**.

## Status at close — every completed task re-verified against the repository

Not re-read. Executed: the suite (114/0), the arithmetic pass (97/97), the
decision paper (65/65); the withdrawn 2.0×/4.1× pair confirmed absent as a live
claim in both documents; `roi.py` constants read back from the module ($999,750
expected cost, 4.8/1.5 h MTTD); the replication module built a real series and
`inspect` verified it, then **detected** both a manifest edit and the extra-field
case; the rebuilt workbook reopened and its cached values checked ($370,000
pilot, ROI 2.0653).

**The workbook swap was completed on 2026-11-10 after Excel released its lock.**
`AxiomDynamics-ROI-Calculator.xlsx` in the docket is now the corrected file —
$370,000 pilot year, three-year ROI 2.0653×, agreeing with A2 §5.1. The
intermediate `…rebuilt.xlsx` and `REPLACE-WORKBOOK.bat` were deleted once the
swap was confirmed byte-identical, because a second copy of the same workbook
under a different name is how the staleness got missed in the first place.

## Transcript — chat-4 extracted and committed at close, 2026-11-10

The standing rule is that a phase is not finished until its assets and its
conversation are in this repository. Chat-4's raw log was extracted at close:
5,667 events, 12 MB, into
`project-logs/transcripts/raw/2026-11-10-chat-4-snapshot.jsonl`, with the
readable extract at `project-logs/transcripts/2026-11-10-chat-4.md` — 704 turns
of which **six are the owner's**.

**A defect in the extractor was fixed in this pass.** `extract_transcript.py`
wrote a hard-coded `"# Chat-3"` heading into every extract regardless of which
session it was processing, so chat-4's file opened under the wrong title. It now
derives the heading from the output filename (`…-chat-4.md` → `# Chat-4`) and
falls back to the filename stem otherwise.

**Build history regenerated at 34 pages.** Part VII still described Findings 1
and 2 as open, which had been true when written in chat-3 and stopped being true
in phase 2 of chat-4. Both are now recorded as closed, with their resolution and
the reasoning kept rather than deleted. Stage 8 was extended to carry the model
decision, and the status-at-a-glance table was corrected — its test count, its
replication row and its commercial-numbers row were all stale.

## Signed ledger export — built 2026-11-10 (AD-3 part two), commit `d9c83d4`

`backend/ledger_export.py` builds an HMAC-SHA256-signed bundle: manifest (id
range, record count, head hash, the ledger's own head, covered-field list,
canonicalisation rule, chain status, previous bundle digest), every record in
canonical form, and a signature over the whole. `tools/verify_ledger_export.py`
verifies it **without importing anything from `backend/`**, from an empty
directory, with `-I` — the recipient needs the bundle, the key, and a Python
standard library, nothing else.

**Why HMAC and not Ed25519:** the stdlib has no asymmetric primitive, and
hand-rolling one in a product that tells CISOs it does not hand-roll crypto
would be worse than the gap. The two limits — cannot name the signer, cannot
date itself — are stated in B01 §4.5a rather than footnoted.

**The audit caught a serious hole, and this is the part worth remembering.**
The first version let a total wipe verify green: delete every row, export
honestly, and a recipient holding the previous bundle was told everything
passed. Each check was individually correct; none compared the bundle against
one already held. Fixed by recording the ledger's own head in every bundle and
failing when a later bundle reports a shorter ledger (`no_truncation`), plus
`genesis_anchor` for rows deleted from the front. Export tests are now 43; the
suite at the time of that build was 80. Three tests assert a failure to detect on purpose, recording disclosed
limits rather than hiding them.

**What it does not do:** detect a ledger wiped before the first bundle in a
series; replicate off-box on a schedule; name the signer. D09 §4.5 makes bundle
retention and a written key-custody procedure the controls that carry that
weight.

Internal account: `assets/ledger-export-build-2026-11-09.md`.

## Transcript — re-snapshotted and committed 2026-11-10, commit `53ad93a`

The standing rule is that a phase is not finished until its assets and its
conversation are in this repository. The chat-3 raw log was re-snapshotted at
close (5,032 events, 17.1 MB) into
`project-logs/transcripts/raw/2026-11-10-chat-3-snapshot.jsonl`, and the
readable extract rebuilt from it — 641 turns, of which **ten are the owner's**;
everything else is assistant text and tool calls.

The mid-session snapshot was deleted rather than kept: it was byte-for-byte a
prefix of the new one, so keeping it would have added 13 MB and no information.
The extractor now lives in the repo at `project-logs/extract_transcript.py`
instead of a shell heredoc, with the rules and the trap that cost a cycle on the
first attempt written into it — the role is the top-level `type` field, not
`message["role"]`.

## Append-only disposition ledger — built 2026-11-09 (AD-3)

The gap that had been disclosed in six documents since `cf2e6ba` is closed at
the code level.

- `backend/store.py` rewritten. Records are inserted, never updated. A second
  decision on an advisory is a new row carrying `supersedes_id`; the earlier row
  keeps its content and timestamp. `BEFORE UPDATE` and `BEFORE DELETE` triggers
  `RAISE(ABORT)`, so the guarantee lives in the schema rather than in convention.
  Every row stores `prev_hash` and `record_hash` — a SHA-256 over its own
  canonical content plus the predecessor's hash — and `verify_chain()`
  recomputes the whole chain and names the first row that fails.
- Migration from the v1 one-row-per-advisory table runs inside `init_db()`,
  preserves the surviving decision and its original timestamp, and does not
  fabricate history that the old schema had already destroyed.
- 17 adversarial tests in `tests/test_store.py`: an UPDATE, a DELETE, a second
  disposition, a tampered row, a removed row, and two migration shapes. Each
  asserts the attempt fails or is detected. `tests/run_tests.py` now discovers
  every `test_*.py`, so the total suite is 38.
- New routes: `GET /api/warrant/{id}/disposition` (full trail, with `chain_ok`)
  and `GET /api/ledger/verify`. The dashboard shows the decision trail under the
  form and marks a corrected decision as superseding an earlier record.

**What it does not prove, and the docket now says so in these words:** the chain
is tamper-*evident*, not tamper-*proof*. A party with write access to the
database file can drop the triggers, rewrite rows and recompute every hash. That
is why items 6 and 8 above stay open.

Docket corrected in the same commit: B01 §4 and §7 items 2/8, D09 §4.4 and the
audit-logging row, F09 Part 6 and Part 7, F00, B02, C02, D12, D14 §5, D00 Part V
and Part VI, and the root README.

## A1 builder — fixed in chat-3

Two defects in `A1-ROI-MODEL/build_roi_calculator.py`, both cosmetic to the
workbook but both real if anyone runs it:

- The sheet-5 assumptions note attributed a **2% catastrophic escalation rate** to
  a model whose cell B17 has held **0.05%** since the correction. A reader
  reconciling the sheet against its own footnote would find a ten-fold conflict.
- The script saved to `/sessions/.../mnt/outputs/...`, a path inside the destroyed
  chat-1 sandbox, so running it raised `FileNotFoundError`. It now writes beside
  itself.


## Git state

The sandbox **cannot reach GitHub** — `git push` and `git fetch` both fail with
HTTP 403 from the proxy. Its `origin/main` ref therefore only advances when the
owner pushes and the sandbox is told the result. Do not trust it as evidence of
remote state without checking the commits page.

**Pushing is done by the owner**, with `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the repo root. It
prints the commits waiting to go up and verifies afterwards.

**Last confirmed pushed state, 2026-11-10:** the owner's push moved the remote to
`bb99cdd`. Everything after it is local and waiting, and every edit to this file
adds to the queue — so the count is deliberately not written here. Run
`git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`.

**The host repo at `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` is authoritative for push state.**
Verify by opening the commits page.

**The line-ending trap.** `git status` in this repo lists nearly every tracked file
as modified on a fresh Windows checkout. It is CRLF working-tree content against
LF blobs, not a content change — `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` returns empty.
There is no `.gitattributes` and `core.autocrlf` is unset. **Always check with
`--ignore-cr-at-eol` before believing a diff stat**, and never let an editor
rewrite a whole file's endings into a commit: doing so once during chat-3 turned a
two-line fix into 1,248 changed lines, which had to be reset and recommitted.


## What was lost in the chat-1 → chat-2 transition

Recorded here so nobody goes looking for it:

- Three commits built at the end of chat-1 (`0b66d21`, `cb4f74d`, and the
  F00/D07/Q6 work) existed only in the old sandbox. **`F00` Rule 7, the D07 §14
  rewrite and Q6 were rebuilt into the repository in chat-2.** The project-logs
  structure was rebuilt. The transcripts were not and cannot be — see
  `README.md`.
- Because the rebuild is a reconstruction rather than a recovery, the wording may
  differ from what chat-1 wrote. The *decisions* are identical; the prose is not
  guaranteed to be. Do not treat the current text as a restoration of an earlier
  draft.

## Standing instructions

- **[WORK LOCATION] All project work is written directly into this repository, first pass, and committed in the same pass.** No drafts in sandbox scratch space — that is how chat-1's final phase was lost.
- Keep the same concept throughout — consistency of framing across every document.
- Internal analysis goes in `assets/`, never `client-assets/`.
- Verify against the file before writing the claim.

## Why chat-1's work was lost — the mechanism

Not a deletion. The work was never on the owner's machine.

Chat-1 built the repo inside a temporary sandbox container. To get anything out
it bundled the repo, embedded the bundle in a `.bat`, and the owner ran it once —
which is how `de9b245` reached GitHub. **Everything chat-1 did after that push
stayed in the container**, including the F00 Rule 7 work, the D07 §14 rewrite, Q6
and the transcripts. The bundle was never remade. When the session ended the
container was destroyed and took all of it.

The failure was treating "committed" as "safe." Inside that container it only
meant "saved somewhere that is about to be emptied."

**The rule that follows:** there is no automatic export. A commit in the sandbox
is not durable until it is in `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` and pushed. Never tell
the owner work is saved without saying where it physically is.

=== chat-4 SUMMARY: last 60 lines ===

## The workbook — rebuilt, not installed

The corrected A1 workbook was built and recalculated with LibreOffice: pilot year
**$370,000** (was $285,000, omitting two A2 lines), three-year ROI **2.0653×**.
At close it could not replace the original because **Excel held a lock on it** —
copy, delete and move all failed with Permission denied even after
`allow_cowork_file_delete`, because the lock is the host application and not a
sandbox permission. It was therefore left beside the original as
`AxiomDynamics-ROI-Calculator.rebuilt.xlsx` with `REPLACE-WORKBOOK.bat` to swap
it in.

**That swap has since run.** Excel released the lock, the corrected file was
copied over the original, the two confirmed byte-identical, and both
intermediates deleted. The docket `.xlsx` now charges $370,000 and returns
2.0653×, agreeing with A2 §5.1. The stale `$285,000` / 2.25× workbook described
below is history, not state.

## The tenth defect, found by validating the completed work

Before closing, the owner asked that the completed tasks be *validated*. That
meant attacking the artifacts rather than re-reading them — and it found one the
two adversarial audits had missed.

**A signed bundle accepted an arbitrary top-level field.** Add any key beside
`format` / `manifest` / `records` / `signature` and both verifiers reported
`ok=True`. Cause: the signature covers a selected tuple and the digest names its
fields; neither covers "everything else", so the added key rode along **unsigned**.
It could be changed after signing with nothing noticing, and a recipient reading
it would reasonably take it as attested by the bundle it sits in.

Both verifiers now fail with `bundle_no_extras` and stop. The signing
construction was left alone — selecting named fields is the right way to sign,
because it makes the covered set explicit in code rather than implicit in the
document. The defect was that verification never checked for anything outside
that set. One test added, mutation-tested in both files: red when the check is
neutered (113 passed, 1 failed), green on restore (114 passed, 0 failed).

**Why this is worth recording.** Nine defects here came from two adversarial
audits. This one came from *trying the thing* rather than reading it, which is a
different act. A green suite says the tests you thought of pass.

## Close of chat-4

Transcript extracted and re-extracted as the session grew, finally at **704 turns
(7 user, 697 assistant)** into `project-logs/transcripts/2026-11-10-chat-4.md`,
with the raw log at `project-logs/transcripts/raw/2026-11-10-chat-4-snapshot.jsonl`
(12.6 MB, 5,667 events). The extract was taken after the last exchange, not before
it — the first attempt missed 110 turns and 3.7 MB of log by snapshotting early.
The extractor's hard-coded `# Chat-3` heading was replaced with a title derived
from the output filename so it cannot mislabel a session again.

Build history regenerated at 34 pages. Part VII was rewritten rather than left
alone: it still described Findings 1 and 2 as open, which had been true when
written in chat-3 and stopped being true in phase 2 of this session. That is the
same defect class the document records elsewhere — a claim that was true when
written and never revisited when the evidence moved.

Verification at close: **114 tests, 97 arithmetic checks, 65 decision-paper
checks — all green.**

# Chat-4 — Summary

Status: **closed 2026-11-10.** Handoff for the next session is
`project-logs/chat-5/CARRY-FORWARD.md`.
Opened with the chat-3 carry-forward. Its first act was to verify the inherited
state against the repository rather than trust the handoff, per the standing rule.

## Verification of inherited state (start of chat-4)

The carry-forward named a remote ref of `bb99cdd` with work waiting on top of it.
Checked with git: the local ref stood at `4eafe58` with one commit above it, so
the written push list was stale again — the fourth session running in which that
happened. Everything else in the handoff held. The CRLF trap was confirmed still
present and still not a content change.

## Phase 1 — the ledger replication series

`backend/ledger_replication.py` executes the cadence D09 §4.5.4 already
specified: monthly full export, weekly incremental chained by
`previous_export_hash`, zero-record weeks kept rather than skipped, nothing ever
overwritten. `inspect` opens every bundle, recomputes its digest, verifies it
against its predecessor, and reports a missing period. 32 tests; the suite went
from 80 to 112. Commit `5ce18cd`; record in
`assets/ledger-replication-build-2026-11-10.md`.

**It deliberately transmits nothing.** D09 §3.2 promises the Platform has no
outbound network, so off-box carriage stays the Railroad's physical step under
§3.3. The owner chose on-box scheduling plus physical carriage over a network
push on 2026-11-10 — the alternative would have meant contradicting a
customer-facing commitment in order to close a control gap. Both docket rows
(B01 §7 item 12, D09 §4.4) now say carriage remains open instead of implying
replication is finished.

**Two audits found nine material defects before this was called built.** The
release verifier rejected every legitimate chained export; `inspect` never
opened a bundle, so tampering read as "continuous"; the period walker hung
forever on a 53-week ISO year (2026 is one); `due_exports` read state outside
the lock so concurrent runs duplicated bundles; and one test passed only because
the check it guarded had been deleted. A green suite of 108 preceded all of it.

## Phase 2 — the model decision, and the 29× defect under it

The owner delegated the A1-versus-D08 question ("you decide"). **A1 governs**, as
Option D in `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md`. Commit `58bfaef`.

A2 §3.2 and D08 §3 now state **1.77× at 500 axles, 3.36× at 10,000** with the
cost basis written into the sentence rather than left to inference, plus the
**1.65× / 3.34×** fallback for a basis that also disallows the conversion credit.

D08 §5–§6 were restated from A1, and the restatement surfaced something the old
headline hid. **D08 §2 scopes the pilot at 100–200 axles**; the old §5 computed a
pilot-year benefit at 500. At 200 axles A1 gives $278,670 against a $370,000
fee — **0.75×. The pilot does not pay for itself at its own scoped fleet size**,
and the document now says so in those words. Production years at 500 axles:
$696,675/yr. Four-year return 2.01×; six-year 2.06× — close to flat, because fee
escalation from Year 4 nearly cancels the dilution of one weak pilot year.

**`backend/roi.py` was valuing a missed defect 29× too high** — it carried a 2%
catastrophic-escalation probability where A1's B17 has held 0.05% since the first
correction, and blended the $9.25M severe-tier midpoint as though it were the
typical cost. It is now **$999,750**, arithmetically identical to A1's B22. The
NTSB benchmarks survive as `SEVERE_FAILURE_COST_*`, reference-only, and the
dataclass field was renamed `severe_cost_range_usd` so no later reader mistakes
them for the typical case.

## The lesson this session added

**The ROI test could not fail.** It rebuilt its expected value from the same
constants it then compared against:
`expected = (1 - roi.P_CAT) * roi.TYPICAL + roi.P_CAT * roi.CATASTROPHIC`,
asserted equal to `roi.EXPECTED_COST_PER_MISSED_DEFECT_USD`, which *is* that
expression. Restoring the 2% defect produced **112 passed, 0 failed**. It now
asserts literals; the same mutation gives 111 passed, 1 failed.

Third session running in which an audit found a test passing for the wrong
reason, and the second in which the faulty test was one I had just written. The
rule that follows is already in memory: assert literals, then break the thing
deliberately and confirm red.

## Nine audit findings, fixed before commit

No — and that's worth being precise about, because the two axes are being conflated by the way the handoffs are written.

What exists in the repo is **priority order, numbered 1–5** in `CURRENT-STATE.md` and again in the carry-forward. Those numbers rank *what blocks what*, not effort. A thing can be priority 1 and small, or priority 5 and enormous. There is no complexity scale anywhere for build items — I checked. The only Low/Medium/High scale in the docket is D06 §2, and that's support-ticket severity (response times for "documentation is unclear" versus "platform down"), not engineering effort.

The single complexity signal that does exist is prose, and it's a warning rather than a rating: the carry-forward says of signer attribution, *"It is much larger than it looks. Do not start here casually."*

Here's my own read, clearly labelled as mine and not the repo's:

| Item | My complexity | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **D07 §14.5 + Phase 0 drafting** | **Low** to produce, **unclosable** by me | I can put the venue decision and formation checklist in front of counsel ready to sign. I can't make the legal call, so it never reaches "done" on my side. |
| **Audit what's built** | **Medium** | No new surface, bounded scope — but unpredictable yield. The tenth defect was found this way and took minutes; the nine before it took two full audits. |
| **Detector ingest path** | **Medium-high**, and it decomposes | Largest product gap, but it breaks into schema → endpoint → validation chain → persistence → tests. The first slice is genuinely small. |
| **SBOM / hash pinning / signed releases** | **Medium each**, three separate jobs | Q1–Q2 2027 targets. Independent of each other, which makes them good fill-in work. |
| **Signer attribution** | **High** — highest on the list | The carry-forward isn't being modest. It needs real local accounts, a key per reviewer, key custody, and it *changes the export bundle format* — so it reopens the verifier, the release verifier, and the tests around them. |

The honest ranking by effort is the reverse of the priority ranking at the top: the item the handoff flags as most important to close is also the one it warns you off starting casually.

If you want something that produces a visible result this session, the ingest path's first slice or the audit are the two that fit. If you want the business side moving while code waits, the formation drafting is cheap and I can do it well. Which way do you want to lean?

**13.2** The Railroad confirms it is not located in, owned or controlled by a person in, a comprehensively sanctioned jurisdiction, and is not a denied party.

**13.3** Supplier confirms the Platform contains no encryption beyond that supplied by the operating system and standard libraries, to Supplier's knowledge, that would require export authorisation.

**13.4** The Railroad shall not export the Platform to any jurisdiction requiring authorisation without obtaining it.

## 14. Dispute resolution

**14.1 Negotiation.** Authorised representatives negotiate in good faith for thirty (30) days from written notice of dispute.

**14.2 Mediation.** If unresolved, mediation under [the mediation rules of the chosen provider] before a single mediator, for a further thirty (30) days. The mediation provider is selected at the same time as the governing law and seat under §14.5.

**14.3 Proceedings.** If unresolved after §14.1 and §14.2, the dispute is determined in the forum identified by §14.5. **Either party may seek injunctive relief at any time** to protect confidentiality or IP, in any court of competent jurisdiction, without waiving this section.

**14.4 Continuing performance.** Both parties continue to perform during a dispute, and the Railroad continues to pay undisputed amounts.

**14.5 Governing law, seat and forum — an open item requiring counsel decision.**

> **This is a decision, not a blank.** The law that governs this Agreement, and the forum in which a dispute is determined, are not stated here because they have not yet been chosen. Treating that as a fill-in blank would misrepresent an unmade decision as a settled one (F00 Rule 7). It is written as what it is.

**(a) What must be decided.** Three things, together: the **governing law** (the substantive law applied), the **seat or forum** (the courts, or the arbitral seat and institution), and the **mediation provider** under §14.2.

**(b) Who decides and by when.** The decision is made by the Supplier with advice of counsel qualified in the candidate jurisdiction, **before this Agreement is first executed with any customer**, and it is recorded in a signed addendum to this Agreement. It cannot be left to the Order: an Order is a commercial instrument and its signatories are not the parties who should be choosing a forum.

**(c) Default expectation, stated as an expectation and not as a term.** Texas law and a Texas venue are the working assumption, because the Supplier is a Texas entity and the counterparties are Texas-headquartered Class I carriers — a Texan forum is the least surprising to both. **This is not the governing law of any Agreement until (b) is done.** A default assumption recorded in a footnote is guidance to counsel; it is not a term a party may enforce.

**(d) What happens if an Order is executed and §14.5 is still open.** The Order is not void, and the parties are not left without a forum. In that event, and only in that event, the dispute is brought in the courts of the state of the Supplier's principal place of business, applying the law of that state, and §14.1–§14.4 apply unchanged. This fallback exists so that an administrative omission cannot be argued as an absence of jurisdiction — but it is a fallback, not a preference, and its use is itself evidence that (b) was not completed.

> **Why this section was rebuilt.** §14.3 previously read: "[the courts / arbitration seat] stated in the Order signature block________ have exclusive jurisdiction." No Order template in this docket contains such a field. The clause therefore pointed at something that did not exist, and a reader checking it would find nothing to check. It also described an unmade decision in the grammar of a settled one. §14 now separates the mechanical parts of dispute resolution, which are decided, from the jurisdictional choice, which is not — and says plainly which is which.

**14.6 Cost of dispute.** Each party bears its own costs unless the forum awards costs.

## 15. Term, termination, and exit

**15.1 Term.** This Agreement begins on execution and continues until terminated.

**15.2 Termination for cause.** Either party on thirty days' notice of material breach uncured.

**15.3 Termination for insolvency.** Immediately on insolvency, administration, or cessation of business of the other.

1	# Q6 — Entity Formation, Support Boundary, and Corridor Strategy
2	
3	**Docket position:** None. **Internal analysis — not for customer distribution.** This document is reasoning for the Supplier's own decisions. It is deliberately *not* in `client-assets/`, and it should not be attached to any Order, brief, or proposal.
4	
5	**Classification:** Internal. Commercially sensitive.
6	
7	**Companion documents:** D04 (SOW-3 discovery terms) · D06 §1.4 (support boundary) · D13 (IP and assignment) · D14 §3 (what AxiomDynamics does not do)
8	
9	---
10	
11	## 1. The question, and the answer in one paragraph
12	
13	Three linked questions get asked at the same time and pull in different directions: **what legal form should the company take, where should it be formed, and how does a support function operate without quietly becoming an operating one?** The answers are: a **Texas LLC** now, converting to a Delaware C-corporation only when a specific trigger fires; formation is **not** the main thing protecting the business and should not be treated as though it were; and the support boundary is a **language problem before it is a policy problem**, which is why §7 is built around sentences an engineer can actually say at 17:55 rather than around a policy document.
14	
15	---
16	
17	## 2. Entity form — LLC, and the reason is thinner than it looks
18	
19	**Recommendation: form as a Texas limited liability company.**
20	
21	The honest version of why: an LLC is the cheapest correct answer for a company that has not raised institutional money, and everything a C-corporation offers is either irrelevant now or purchasable later at a known price.
22	
23	- **Pass-through taxation.** An LLC is taxed once, at the members. For a pre-revenue company whose near-term problem is runway, not distribution, this matters and a C-corp's double taxation does not.
24	- **Cheap to run.** No board, no formal minutes requirement imposed by statute, no shareholder register to maintain. An early-stage company that spends its governance budget on governance has spent it on the wrong thing.
25	- **Conversion is routine, not a rebuild.** Converting a Texas LLC to a Delaware C-corporation is a well-trodden path. It costs a few thousand dollars in legal and filing fees and is not a reason to form the wrong entity now. **A company that forms a C-corp to be "ready for investors" has paid for a structure it may never need.**
26	
27	**What an LLC does not give you, stated plainly.** It does not protect against *personal* liability for the company's own torts committed by the member, it does not survive a failure to observe formalities, and — the point that matters most here — **it does not protect anything that a counterparty has made you personally guarantee.** See §4.
28	
29	---
30	
31	## 3. Where to form — Texas, not Delaware
32	
33	**Recommendation: Texas.**
34	
35	The generic advice is Delaware, and the generic advice is wrong here for reasons specific to this company rather than generic ones.
36	
37	**The Delaware argument is about the Court of Chancery.** It is a specialist court for shareholder litigation — disputes among founders, between a board and its investors, over fiduciary duty. **AxiomDynamics, as an LLC with no outside investors, has none of that litigation.** Delaware's principal advantage is insurance against a risk the company does not currently carry.
38	
39	**The Delaware argument is also about investor familiarity.** That is a real benefit, and it is the reason the conversion trigger in §5 exists. It is not a reason to pay Delaware's annual tax and registered-agent fees for years before the first institutional cheque.
40	
41	**The Texas argument is about the counterparties.** This docket is written for Texas-headquartered Class I carriers. A Texas entity contracting with a Texas carrier is the least surprising arrangement to a procurement department, and if litigation ever happens, a Texas forum is where it would be least expensive to conduct. That is a modest advantage, but it is a real one and it points the same way as cost.
42	
43	**On the corridor, not the registered office.** The customer relationships span multiple carriers across multiple states. Nothing about where the entity is registered changes the operating footprint. Registration is a legal address, not a market presence, and a Texas registration does not tilt the commercial strategy toward any one carrier.
44	
45	### Verified formation and maintenance costs
46	
47	Checked against official sources rather than recalled. Where a figure could not be settled, it says so.
48	
49	| Item | Amount | Source | Status |
50	|---|---|---|---|
51	| Texas LLC Certificate of Formation (Form 205) | **$300** one-time | Texas Secretary of State, Form 205 instructions | Verified |
52	| Texas name reservation (optional) | $40 | Texas SOS | Verified |
53	| Texas franchise tax | **$0** below the no-tax-due threshold | Texas Comptroller, 2026 Form 05-915 | Verified — see below |
54	| 2026 no-tax-due threshold | **$2,650,000** annualized total revenue | Texas Comptroller 2026 instructions | Verified — up from $2.47M for the 2025 report |
55	| Texas foreign-entity registration (Form 304), if needed | **$750** | Texas SOS fee schedule (Form 806) | Verified |
56	| Delaware LLC annual tax | **$300 or $400 for 2026 — conflicting** | Delaware Division of Corporations | **Unresolved** — see below |
57	
58	**On the franchise tax.** A Texas LLC below $2.65M in annualized total revenue owes no franchise tax. It still files the Public Information Report annually to remain in good standing. A new entity is not required to file a No Tax Due Report in its first five years. Reports are due **15 May**. **The obligation to file does not disappear because the tax is zero** — the most common way a small company loses good standing is by treating "no tax due" as "no filing."
59	
60	**On the Delaware figure, honestly.** Sources conflict for tax year 2026: the Division of Revenue's older guidance and several guides still state a flat **$300**, while recently published sources and the Division of Corporations' own LLC/LP/GP instructions page reference **$400**. I am not going to pick one to make the table look tidy. The correct action is to read `corp.delaware.gov` at the moment of decision, and the table above should be read as "a few hundred dollars a year, confirm before relying on it." **This does not affect the recommendation**, because the recommendation is not to register in Delaware at all.
61	
62	**Additional real costs not in the table**, because they are not government fees and vary too much to state usefully: registered agent (roughly $50–$300/year in Texas), and counsel review of the operating agreement, which is the item worth actually paying for. The filing fee is the cheapest part of forming a company and the least important.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## 4. The thing that will actually erase the protection
67	
68	Formation is not the main risk to the liability shield, and treating it as though it were is the most common mistake in this analysis.
69	
70	**The most likely way to lose the protection on the largest exposure is a personal guarantee.** A Class I carrier's procurement function will, on a vendor with no balance sheet, ask the principal to guarantee obligations personally — payment, indemnity, or performance. A guarantee converts a limited liability company into a personal exposure for exactly the obligations that matter most. **No amount of correct entity formation survives it.** A signature on a guarantee is the single most consequential document this company will sign, and it is usually signed by someone who thinks of it as paperwork.
71	
72	The position:
73	
74	- **A guarantee of payment obligations should be refused** wherever possible. If a carrier requires assurance, offer instead: a larger pilot credit, a performance bond, an escrow, or a staged payment schedule that limits the carrier's exposure to value not yet delivered.
75	- **A guarantee of indemnity for third-party personal injury is the one to think hardest about.** It is also the one a carrier will press hardest for. It should never be signed without counsel, and never as a schedule to an Order signed by an engineer.
76	- **Whoever signs must know they are signing personally.** A guarantee signed on the assumption that "it's the company's contract" is a guarantee that will be enforced against a person who did not understand it.
77	
78	The second way the shield fails is **commingling and informality** — paying company expenses from a personal account, no operating agreement, no separation of records. This is cheap to avoid and expensive to discover. The single highest-value spend in the formation process is a proper operating agreement reviewed by counsel, not the filing fee.
79	
80	**This is not legal advice, and it should not be treated as a substitute for counsel admitted in the relevant jurisdiction.** The specific question of whether a guarantee is enforceable in a given form, against a given signatory, in a given state, is precisely what counsel is for.
81	
82	---
83	
84	## 5. When to convert to a Delaware C-corporation
85	
86	Concrete triggers, so the decision is made by an event rather than by a feeling:
87	
88	1. **An institutional equity round is being raised.** Convert before the term sheet, not after — the round documents will assume a Delaware C-corp.
89	2. **A stock-based option pool is wanted for employees.** LLC profits interests can work but are awkward; a C-corp with options is the conventional instrument.
90	3. **An acquisition approach arrives.** A buyer will usually want a C-corp; conversion is fast, but it is faster if planned.
91	
92	Absent one of these, the LLC is the correct and cheaper structure. **Do not convert in anticipation of a round that has no lead investor.**
93	
94	---
95	
96	## 6. What this section does not decide
97

**Classification:** Internal. Commercially sensitive.

**Companion documents:** D04 (SOW-3 discovery terms) · D06 §1.4 (support boundary) · D13 (IP and assignment) · D14 §3 (what AxiomDynamics does not do)

---

## 1. The question, and the answer in one paragraph

Three linked questions get asked at the same time and pull in different directions: **what legal form should the company take, where should it be formed, and how does a support function operate without quietly becoming an operating one?** The answers are: a **Texas LLC** now, converting to a Delaware C-corporation only when a specific trigger fires; formation is **not** the main thing protecting the business and should not be treated as though it were; and the support boundary is a **language problem before it is a policy problem**, which is why §7 is built around sentences an engineer can actually say at 17:55 rather than around a policy document.

---

## 2. Entity form — LLC, and the reason is thinner than it looks

**Recommendation: form as a Texas limited liability company.**

The honest version of why: an LLC is the cheapest correct answer for a company that has not raised institutional money, and everything a C-corporation offers is either irrelevant now or purchasable later at a known price.

- **Pass-through taxation.** An LLC is taxed once, at the members. For a pre-revenue company whose near-term problem is runway, not distribution, this matters and a C-corp's double taxation does not.
- **Cheap to run.** No board, no formal minutes requirement imposed by statute, no shareholder register to maintain. An early-stage company that spends its governance budget on governance has spent it on the wrong thing.
- **Conversion is routine, not a rebuild.** Converting a Texas LLC to a Delaware C-corporation is a well-trodden path. It costs a few thousand dollars in legal and filing fees and is not a reason to form the wrong entity now. **A company that forms a C-corp to be "ready for investors" has paid for a structure it may never need.**

**What an LLC does not give you, stated plainly.** It does not protect against *personal* liability for the company's own torts committed by the member, it does not survive a failure to observe formalities, and — the point that matters most here — **it does not protect anything that a counterparty has made you personally guarantee.** See §4.

---

## 3. Where to form — Texas, not Delaware

**Recommendation: Texas.**

The generic advice is Delaware, and the generic advice is wrong here for reasons specific to this company rather than generic ones.

**The Delaware argument is about the Court of Chancery.** It is a specialist court for shareholder litigation — disputes among founders, between a board and its investors, over fiduciary duty. **AxiomDynamics, as an LLC with no outside investors, has none of that litigation.** Delaware's principal advantage is insurance against a risk the company does not currently carry.

**The Delaware argument is also about investor familiarity.** That is a real benefit, and it is the reason the conversion trigger in §5 exists. It is not a reason to pay Delaware's annual tax and registered-agent fees for years before the first institutional cheque.

**The Texas argument is about the counterparties.** This docket is written for Texas-headquartered Class I carriers. A Texas entity contracting with a Texas carrier is the least surprising arrangement to a procurement department, and if litigation ever happens, a Texas forum is where it would be least expensive to conduct. That is a modest advantage, but it is a real one and it points the same way as cost.

**On the corridor, not the registered office.** The customer relationships span multiple carriers across multiple states. Nothing about where the entity is registered changes the operating footprint. | Item | Amount | Source | Status |

| Texas name reservation (optional) | $40 | Texas SOS | Verified |
| Texas franchise tax | **$0** below the no-tax-due threshold | Texas Comptroller, 2026 Form 05-915 | Verified — see below |
| 2026 no-tax-due threshold | **$2,650,000** annualized total revenue | Texas Comptroller 2026 instructions | Verified — up from $2.47M for the 2025 report |
| Texas foreign-entity registration (Form 304), if needed | **$750** | Texas SOS fee schedule (Form 806) | Verified |
| Delaware LLC annual tax | **$300 or $400 for 2026 — conflicting** | Delaware Division of Corporations | **Unresolved** — see below |

**On the franchise tax.** A Texas LLC below $2.65M in annualized total revenue owes no franchise tax. It still files the Public Information Report annually to remain in good standing. A new entity is not required to file a No Tax Due Report in its first five years. Reports are due **15 May**. **The obligation to file does not disappear because the tax is zero** — the most common way a small company loses good standing is by treating "no tax due" as "no filing."

**On the Delaware figure, honestly.** Sources conflict for tax year 2026: the Division of Revenue's older guidance and several guides still state a flat **$300**, while recently published sources and the Division of Corporations' own LLC/LP/GP instructions page reference **$400**. I am not going to pick one to make the table look tidy. The correct action is to read `corp.delaware.gov` at the moment of decision, and the table above should be read as "a few hundred dollars a year, confirm before relying on it." **This does not affect the recommendation**, because the recommendation is not to register in Delaware at all.

**Additional real costs not in the table**, because they are not government fees and vary too much to state usefully: registered agent (roughly $50–$300/year in Texas), and counsel review of the operating agreement, which is the item worth actually paying for. The filing fee is the cheapest part of forming a company and the least important.

---

## 4. The thing that will actually erase the protection

Formation is not the main risk to the liability shield, and treating it as though it were is the most common mistake in this analysis.

**The most likely way to lose the protection on the largest exposure is a personal guarantee.** A Class I carrier's procurement function will, on a vendor with no balance sheet, ask the principal to guarantee obligations personally — payment, indemnity, or performance. A guarantee converts a limited liability company into a personal exposure for exactly the obligations that matter most. **No amount of correct entity formation survives it.** A signature on a guarantee is the single most consequential document this company will sign, and it is usually signed by someone who thinks of it as paperwork.

The position:

- **A guarantee of payment obligations should be refused** wherever possible. If a carrier requires assurance, offer instead: a larger pilot credit, a performance bond, an escrow, or a staged payment schedule that limits the carrier's exposure to value not yet delivered.
- **A guarantee of indemnity for third-party personal injury is the one to think hardest about.** It is also the one a carrier will press hardest for. It should never be signed without counsel, and never as a schedule to an Order signed by an engineer.
- **Whoever signs must know they are signing personally.** A guarantee signed on the assumption that "it's the company's contract" is a guarantee that will be enforced against a person who did not understand it.

108	The failure mode is not malice or a policy violation. It is a tired engineer on a call at 17:55 with a worried customer, asked a direct question, giving a helpful answer. The helpful answer is the expensive one. **A policy is read at induction; a substitution table is used in the moment.** This is that table.
109	
110	| The customer asks | Do not say | Say instead |
111	|---|---|---|
112	| "Should I pull this car?" | "I would." / "I wouldn't worry." | "The Platform scored this axle at [X] against its own baseline. Whether to pull the car is your operating decision under your rules. I can walk you through how the score was computed." |
113	| "Is this a false alarm?" | "Probably." / "I doubt it's real." | "I can't characterise it as a false alarm — that's a judgement about the asset, and it isn't mine to make. What I can tell you is what the model saw and how confident it is." |
114	| "Would you treat it as a defect?" | "Yes, I'd flag it." | "The Platform has flagged it, and here is the evidence behind the flag. What your inspection finds is the answer to whether it's a defect." |
115	| "What does the regulation require here?" | Anything that sounds like an answer. | "That's your regulatory obligation under your rules, and I'm not able to interpret it. Your compliance group is the right call." |
116	| "Just tell me what to do." | Any instruction. | "I know that's the frustrating answer. I can't make the call for you — but I can get you everything the Platform computed so your call is fast." |
117	| "Can you approve this record?" | Any signature or co-signature. | "I can't sign or co-sign your record. I can confirm what the Platform reported, in writing, in the ticket." |
118	| "Can we talk this through on the phone?" | Substantive advice, verbally. | "Happy to triage on the phone. For anything substantive I'll put it in the ticket so there's a record of what was said — that protects you as much as me." |
119	
120	**Three disciplines that make the table usable:**
121	
122	1. **Record the declination verbatim.** Every ticket touching an advisory closes with the sentence actually used. A consistent pattern of declination across hundreds of tickets is the most persuasive evidence of the operating boundary in any later examination of a decision (D06 §1.4).
123	2. **Written, not verbal.** A ticket proves what was said *and what was not said*. A phone call proves neither.
124	3. **Nobody is the sole responder for two carriers at once** (D06 §7.4). The 17:55 problem is a staffing problem as much as a language problem; the substitution table does not fix a company that has one engineer covering four time zones.
125	
126	**Why this is worth the space.** The boundary is the commercial asset. A support engineer who gives one helpful opinion about one train converts a decision-support product into an advisory service, and an advisory service to a Class I carrier about a train is a regulated activity the company is not structured, insured, or staffed to perform. **The sentence is the product boundary, not the policy document.**
127	
128	---
129	
130	## 8. Corridor strategy — sequencing, not geography
131	
132	The corridor question is really a sequencing question: which customer first, and what does the first one buy that the second one cannot.
133	
134	**Sequence by failure mode, not by carrier size.** The right first customer is the one with a failure mode that the three physical models actually address and data that exists. A Tier 1 carrier with a well-instrumented route and a known bearing problem is worth more as a reference than a larger carrier whose pain point is one the platform cannot see.
135	
136	**The discovery visit is the unit of commitment, and it is priced accordingly.** SOW-3 (D04) is the Feasibility & Physics Assessment at **$45,000–$75,000**, and its structure is deliberate: the deliverable permits "no, and here is why," which is what makes it honest and what makes it sellable. A discovery engagement that can only conclude "yes" is a sales call with an invoice.
137	
138	**What the first customer must produce, in order:** a signed F02 (which starts the pilot clock), a disposition ledger with actual reviewer decisions in it, and a reference the second carrier's Chief Engineer will take a call about. The reference is the asset. The revenue is not, at this stage.
139	
140	**What not to do:** do not run two first customers simultaneously. The support boundary in §7 depends on an engineer who is not spread across two carriers' operating cultures at once, and the first pilot's real output is a set of sentences and processes that the second pilot reuses. Two at once produces two half-built playbooks.
141	
142	---
143	
144	## 9. Summary of recommendations
145	
146	| Decision | Recommendation | Confidence |
147	|---|---|---|
148	| Entity form | Texas LLC | High |
149	| State of formation | Texas | High — Delaware's advantage is litigation the company does not have |
150	| Conversion trigger | Institutional round, option pool, or acquisition approach | High |
151	| Largest threat to the shield | Personal guarantee, not formation mechanics | High — and under-weighted in earlier analysis |
152	| Support boundary | Substitution table, written record, staffing discipline | High |
153	| First corridor | Choose by failure mode and data availability, not carrier size | Medium — depends on which conversations are live |
154	
155	**Two things this document cannot tell you:** which carrier to approach first, because that depends on relationships this document does not see; and the correct venue and governing law, which is D07 §14.5 and is an open counsel decision, not a formation question.
156	
157	---
158	
159	*Internal analysis. Reviewed when the entity form changes, when a guarantee is requested, or annually. Not for customer distribution.*

Search limit reached. Here's what the results support:

## Key finding: the "Chapter 271" premise is off

The forum-selection/out-of-state-venue statute is **not** in the Civil Practice and Remedies Code. Two chapters are actually in play:

**Tex. Bus. & Com. Code ch. 271** — "Rights of Parties to Choose Law Applicable" . It governs written choice-of-law agreements in "qualified transactions" (roughly $1M+) and adds safe harbors for choosing another state's law, effective Sept. 1, 2011 . Note: **Chapter 271 governs choice of *law*, not venue/forum** — the venue clauses sit in Chapter 272.

**Tex. Bus. & Com. Code ch. 272 (esp. § 272.001)** — the real out-of-state forum rule, and only for **construction contracts concerning Texas real property**. As amended (HB 2960, 2023), it now makes out-of-state **forum, venue, choice-of-law, and arbitration** provisions **void as against public policy**, not merely voidable at the obligated party's option . New § 272.001(c) supplies a default: unless the parties stipulate otherwise after the dispute arises, venue defaults to a Texas county under the general venue rules .

**Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code ch. 15** (§ 15.020) — the older, still-relevant CPRC provision on forum/venue in "major transactions," discussed in the practitioner literature alongside Chapter 15's general venue scheme . Also § 15.020 appears in the context of the 2023 construction amendments .

## General Texas enforceability standard

Outside those statutory carve-outs, forum-selection clauses are **presumed valid and enforceable**; the party resisting must clearly show enforcement would be unreasonable or unjust, the clause is invalid for fraud or overreaching, or enforcement would contravene Texas public policy . *In re AutoNation*, 228 S.W.3d 663 (Tex. 2007), is the anchor case . Nonsignatory enforcement is an evolving area .

## Important caveat

The search results muddle two things you should keep separate: **forum** (which sovereign's courts) vs. **venue** (which county within a state) . Texas courts have generally enforced mandatory forum clauses , but a pure venue-selection clause failing to satisfy the statutory venue scheme is a different question .

I'd flag that I couldn't confirm the exact current text of CPRC Chapter 271 or whether § 15.020 has been amended — worth pulling the statute directly from statutes.capitol.texas.gov  before relying on this.

## Key finding: the "Chapter 271" premise is off

The forum-selection/out-of-state-venue statute is **not** in the Civil Practice and Remedies Code. Two chapters are actually in play:

**Tex. Bus. & Com. Code ch. 271** — "Rights of Parties to Choose Law Applicable" . It governs written choice-of-law agreements in "qualified transactions" (roughly $1M+) and adds safe harbors for choosing another state's law, effective Sept. 1, 2011 . Note: **Chapter 271 governs choice of *law*, not venue/forum** — the venue clauses sit in Chapter 272.

**Tex. Bus. & Com. Code ch. 272 (esp. § 272.001)** — the real out-of-state forum rule, and only for **construction contracts concerning Texas real property**. As amended (HB 2960, 2023), it now makes out-of-state **forum, venue, choice-of-law, and arbitration** provisions **void as against public policy**, not merely voidable at the obligated party's option . New § 272.001(c) supplies a default: unless the parties stipulate otherwise after the dispute arises, venue defaults to a Texas county under the general venue rules .

**Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code ch. 15** (§ 15.020) — the older, still-relevant CPRC provision on forum/venue in "major transactions," discussed in the practitioner literature alongside Chapter 15's general venue scheme . Also § 15.020 appears in the context of the 2023 construction amendments .

## General Texas enforceability standard

Outside those statutory carve-outs, forum-selection clauses are **presumed valid and enforceable**; the party resisting must clearly show enforcement would be unreasonable or unjust, the clause is invalid for fraud or overreaching, or enforcement would contravene Texas public policy . *In re AutoNation*, 228 S.W.3d 663 (Tex. 2007), is the anchor case . Nonsignatory enforcement is an evolving area .

## Important caveat

The search results muddle two things you should keep separate: **forum** (which sovereign's courts) vs. **venue** (which county within a state) . Texas courts have generally enforced mandatory forum clauses , but a pure venue-selection clause failing to satisfy the statutory venue scheme is a different question .

I'd flag that I couldn't confirm the exact current text of CPRC Chapter 271 or whether § 15.020 has been amended — worth pulling the statute directly from statutes.capitol.texas.gov  before relying on this.

=== D07 8.1 cap ===
## 8. Liability

**8.1 Cap.** Subject to §8.3, each party's total aggregate liability arising under or in connection with this Agreement, whether in contract, tort (including negligence), breach of statutory duty or otherwise, shall not exceed **the fees paid or payable by the Railroad in the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim**.

> **On the cap, and why there is no floor figure.** An earlier draft capped liability at "the greater of twelve months' fees **or [amount]**," with the amount left blank — and D03 §10 cross-referred to it as an operative term. **A liability clause with an unfilled limb is worse than no clause: it is unenforceable in the place it matters and it invites the other side to propose their own number.** The cap is now a single, complete, calculated figure — twelve months' fees — which at the pilot is $370,000 and at a 2,000-axle production licence is $1,050,000. It requires no blank to be filled and no negotiation to be settled.

**8.2 Excluded loss.** Neither party is liable for loss of profit, revenue, business, contracts, anticipated savings, goodwill, or any indirect or consequential loss, however arising, even if advised of the possibility.

**8.3 Unlimited.** Nothing in this section limits liability for: death or personal injury caused by negligence; fraud or fraudulent misrepresentation; breach of confidentiality; infringement of the other party's intellectual property; or any liability that cannot lawfully be limited.

**8.4 Product liability — stated openly.**

The parties acknowledge that §8.1 allocates contractual risk between commercial parties. **It does not, and cannot, exclude a claim in tort arising from personal injury, death, or damage to property caused by a defective product.** Nothing in this Agreement purports to exclude such liability, and no provision should be read as doing so.

**The parties further acknowledge** that the Platform is a decision-support tool (D12), that the Railroad retains sole operating authority, and that a claim arising from an operating decision made by the Railroad is governed by §8.3 and by the Railroad's own responsibility under D12 §4.

**8.5 Basis of bargain.** The fees reflect the allocation of risk in this section. The Railroad may obtain additional protection through insurance arranged at its own cost.

## 9. Indemnities

## 8. Liability

**8.1 Cap.** Subject to §8.3, each party's total aggregate liability arising under or in connection with this Agreement, whether in contract, tort (including negligence), breach of statutory duty or otherwise, shall not exceed **the fees paid or payable by the Railroad in the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim**.

> **On the cap, and why there is no floor figure.** An earlier draft capped liability at "the greater of twelve months' fees **or [amount]**," with the amount left blank — and D03 §10 cross-referred to it as an operative term. **A liability clause with an unfilled limb is worse than no clause: it is unenforceable in the place it matters and it invites the other side to propose their own number.** The cap is now a single, complete, calculated figure — twelve months' fees — which at the pilot is $370,000 and at a 2,000-axle production licence is $1,050,000. It requires no blank to be filled and no negotiation to be settled.

**8.2 Excluded loss.** Neither party is liable for loss of profit, revenue, business, contracts, anticipated savings, goodwill, or any indirect or consequential loss, however arising, even if advised of the possibility.

**8.3 Unlimited.** Nothing in this section limits liability for: death or personal injury caused by negligence; fraud or fraudulent misrepresentation; breach of confidentiality; infringement of the other party's intellectual property; or any liability that cannot lawfully be limited.

**8.4 Product liability — stated openly.**

The parties acknowledge that §8.1 allocates contractual risk between commercial parties. **It does not, and cannot, exclude a claim in tort arising from personal injury, death, or damage to property caused by a defective product.** Nothing in this Agreement purports to exclude such liability, and no provision should be read as doing so.

**The parties further acknowledge** that the Platform is a decision-support tool (D12), that the Railroad retains sole operating authority, and that a claim arising from an operating decision made by the Railroad is governed by §8.3 and by the Railroad's own responsibility under D12 §4.

**8.5 Basis of bargain.** The fees reflect the allocation of risk in this section. The Railroad may obtain additional protection through insurance arranged at its own cost.
