# Supply Chain — Build Record, 2026-11-11 (chat-5)

**Docket position:** None. **Internal — not for customer distribution.**

**Companion documents:** D09 §4.4, §7.2, §7.3 (the promises), D10 Parts 2 and 5
(the register), C01 Part C2 (the sealed archive), `tools/sbom.py`,
`tools/pin_requirements.py`, `tools/sign_release.py`.

---

## 1. What was open, and what "open" meant

D09 §4.4 carried three rows with 2027 targets: no SBOM in releases, no hash
pinning of dependency downloads, no signed release artefacts. All three are now
built as tools. **Two are not yet applied, and this document is mostly about that
distinction**, because the project has already been burned once by reading
"built" as "done" — B01 §4.5a item 1 promised rewrite-detection that did not
exist, and the sentence survived three audits.

| Control | Tool | Applied? |
|---|---|---|
| SBOM | `tools/sbom.py` | **No** — no release has shipped carrying one |
| Hash pinning | `tools/pin_requirements.py` | **No** — `requirements.txt` is still a range; the build now fails rather than shipping unpinned |
| Signed releases | `tools/sign_release.py` | **No** — no key issued, nothing signed |

## 2. The finding that came out before the code

D10 Part 2 read: *"The complete inventory of third-party code that executes as
part of the Platform. **One component.**"* Then a table with numpy in it.

The numpy binary wheel is not one component. It bundles six more things that
execute inside our process: OpenBLAS, LAPACK, `libgfortran` (GPL-3.0 **with the
GCC Runtime Library Exception**), `libquadmath` (LGPL-2.1-or-later),
`lapack-lite`, `dragon4` and `libdivide`. Two of those carry licences that make a
procurement reviewer stop and read again.

The licences are fine — the GCC runtime exception exists precisely so proprietary
software can link the GCC runtime, and the LGPL is satisfied by dynamic linking,
which is how it ships. The warranty at D07 §3.4 stands. **What was wrong was the
completeness claim**, and it matters for a reason beyond accuracy: a register that
says "one component" and is off by seven is the exact understatement a security
reviewer finds first, and it retroactively casts doubt on every other count in the
document.

Corrected in D10 Part 2, with each bundled library, its licence and what it is.
`tools/sbom.py` now emits the same list from the installed tree, so the table can
be regenerated instead of trusted.

## 3. SBOM — `tools/sbom.py`

CycloneDX 1.5 JSON, written directly rather than with a library, for the same
reason `tools/verify_ledger_export.py` imports nothing from the Platform: a
recipient must be able to read the artefact with a text editor and a JSON parser.
Adding a dependency to generate the document about our dependencies is a joke that
writes itself.

**The digest is a tree hash, not a file hash.** Each component carries a SHA-256
over the sorted list of (relative path, file SHA-256) for every file it installed,
length-prefixed so path and content boundaries cannot be shifted. That is
recomputable on the Railroad's machine from their installed tree, which is what
makes it a verification tool rather than a claim — and it catches a substituted
wheel, because a substituted wheel installs different bytes under the same name
and version.

**Scoping is the design decision worth arguing about.** Run unscoped on this build
host, the tool found 153 distributions — `ufw` (a GPL-3 firewall tool), `Twisted`,
`odfpy`, and plenty else the Platform has never imported. A customer reading that
SBOM would reasonably conclude we ship them. So `generate --requirements` scopes to
the requirement file and its transitive closure; this project's comes out at **one
component**. The unscoped mode still exists because it is useful on a real
deployment host, and it warns by existing without a scope.

**Verification is six checks**: format, spec version, no declared component
missing, no installed component undeclared, tree hash, interpreter version. The
undeclared direction is the dangerous one — an unaccounted dependency is a
dependency nobody reviewed, sitting in the process.

## 4. Hash pinning — `tools/pin_requirements.py`, and a mistake I made

**I wrote two invented SHA-256 strings into `requirements.txt` and committed
nothing.** They looked like digests. They were not digests of anything. Had they
survived, `pip install --require-hashes` would have rejected every real numpy
download, and the failure would have arrived at release time on the Railroad's
machine — the exact outcome the control exists to prevent, caused by the control.

Caught before commit, reverted, and the tool was written so that it cannot happen
again:

- **No `--hash` flag exists.** There is no way to paste a digest in.
- **Every hash comes from `_sha256()` of a file `pip download` just produced**, in
  the same process.
- **`test_no_hash_anywhere_in_this_tool_was_typed_by_a_human`** asserts the tool
  contains no 64-hex-character literal, and the test file asserts the same about
  itself. A future session cannot reintroduce the mistake quietly.
- **A range is refused.** `numpy>=1.26` cannot be hash-pinned, because the index
  may serve any matching file; the tool says so instead of emitting a range with
  no hashes and calling it pinned.

**Why the file is not pinned right now.** The pin step needs index access; this
sandbox's proxy returns 403 to PyPI. So pinning is a release-host step, alongside
C01 Part C2's archive preparation. What changed in the repository is the
enforcement: the **Dockerfile and the release path now pass `--require-hashes`**,
so an unpinned `requirements.txt` **fails the build** instead of installing
whatever the index serves while a comment claims a control.

`render.yaml` deliberately does **not** get the flag. It deploys the public demo
from the public repo over the public internet; nothing it serves is a release
artefact. Breaking the demo would buy no security and cost a working site.

## 5. Signed releases — `tools/sign_release.py`

D09 §7.3 names GPG, so the tool wraps GPG rather than inventing a scheme. The
Railroad's security team already knows `gpg --verify`; asking them to learn ours
would be the same mistake the ledger export avoided by importing nothing.

**Reproducibility is a security property here, not tidiness.** If two builds of
the same content differ, the signature covers the difference — the build machine's
clock and user id become part of what was attested. The tool pins the gzip header
mtime (which `tarfile.open(..., "w:gz")` sets to `time.time()` independently of
the tar contents), normalises uid/gid to root, and sets one fixed mtime on every
entry.

That fix was found by mutation testing, not by reading: **removing both the gzip
mtime and the tar mtime still left the reproducibility test green**, because both
builds happened inside the same second. The test now sleeps 1.2 s between builds,
and the mutation goes red. This is the fourth session running that a green test
turned out not to be guarding anything.

The archive also writes the `MANIFEST.sha256` C01 Part C2 already describes, so
the sealed-archive path gains a signature without gaining a new procedure.

**What a signature does not prove** is in D09 §7.3: it proves the artefact was
signed by the key and has not changed; it does not prove the key was ours unless
the public key arrived by a route the Railroad trusts, and it does not prove the
build has no defect. Key custody carries that weight — exactly as with the export
key under §4.5.

## 6. Verification performed

- Suite **143 → 180, all green**, across three new files: 15 SBOM tests, 12
  pinning tests, 10 release tests.
- **Every guard mutation-tested individually.** Disabling the tree-hash check,
  the undeclared-component check, the declared-component check, the scoping, the
  range refusal, the empty-download guard, the verify mismatch path, the
  signature-failure path, the exclusion filter and the reproducibility fix each
  turned exactly the intended test red.
- **Two tests passed for the wrong reason and were rewritten**, both recorded
  above: the duplicate-key test (caught by the version check, not the loader) and
  the release-contents test (`axiom.db` was never in scope, so excluding it proved
  nothing).
- End-to-end against real GPG 2.2: key generation, build, export public key,
  sign, verify `ok`, append one byte to the archive, verify `FAILED`.
- End-to-end against a real numpy installation: SBOM generated, verified, then
  three attacks — changed tree hash, changed version, ghost component — each
  caught by a distinct named check.

## 7. The lesson this pass adds

**A control has three states, not two: absent, built, and applied. Collapsing the
middle one into either neighbour is how documents start lying.** D09 §7.3 already
had the rule that every gap in §4.4 needs a corresponding statement in §7 — this
pass extends it: the statement must say which of the three states the control is
in. "Implemented" is not a state.

The second, narrower lesson is the one about my own error. Two invented hashes
looked exactly like a pinned file. Nothing in the repository would have caught it
— the tests would have run, the build would have failed much later, on someone
else's machine. What caught it was reading back what I had written before
committing. That is not a process; it is luck with a habit attached, and the
regression test in §4 is the process that replaces it.

---

*Internal. Review when the pin step runs on the release host, when a GPG key is
issued, or when an SBOM ships with a release.*

so an unpinned `requirements.txt` **fails the build** instead of installing
whatever the index serves while a comment claims a control.

`render.yaml` deliberately does **not** get the flag. It deploys the public demo
from the public repo over the public internet; nothing it serves is a release
artefact. Breaking the demo would buy no security and cost a working site.

## 5. Signed releases — `tools/sign_release.py`

D09 §7.3 names GPG, so the tool wraps GPG rather than inventing a scheme. The
Railroad's security team already knows `gpg --verify`; asking them to learn ours
would be the same mistake the ledger export avoided by importing nothing.

**Reproducibility is a security property here, not tidiness.** If two builds of
the same content differ, the signature covers the difference — the build machine's
clock and user id become part of what was attested. The tool pins the gzip header
mtime (which `tarfile.open(..., "w:gz")` sets to `time.time()` independently of
the tar contents), normalises uid/gid to root, and sets one fixed mtime on every
entry.

That fix was found by mutation testing, not by reading: **removing both the gzip
mtime and the tar mtime still left the reproducibility test green**, because both
builds happened inside the same second. The test now sleeps 1.2 s between builds,
and the mutation goes red. This is the fourth session running that a green test
turned out not to be guarding anything.

The archive also writes the `MANIFEST.sha256` C01 Part C2 already describes, so
the sealed-archive path gains a signature without gaining a new procedure.

**What a signature does not prove** is in D09 §7.3: it proves the artefact was
signed by the key and has not changed; it does not prove the key was ours unless
the public key arrived by a route the Railroad trusts, and it does not prove the
build has no defect. Key custody carries that weight — exactly as with the export
key under §4.5.

## 6. Verification performed

- Suite **143 → 180, all green**, across three new files: 15 SBOM tests, 12
  pinning tests, 10 release tests.
- **Every guard mutation-tested individually.** Disabling the tree-hash check,
  the undeclared-component check, the declared-component check, the scoping, the
  range refusal, the empty-download guard, the verify mismatch path, the
  signature-failure path, the exclusion filter and the reproducibility fix each
  turned exactly the intended test red.
- **Two tests passed for the wrong reason and were rewritten**, both recorded
  above: the duplicate-key test (caught by the version check, not the loader) and
  the release-contents test (`axiom.db` was never in scope, so excluding it proved
  nothing).
- End-to-end against real GPG 2.2: key generation, build, export public key,
  sign, verify `ok`, append one byte to the archive, verify `FAILED`.
- End-to-end against a real numpy installation: SBOM generated, verified, then
  three attacks — changed tree hash, changed version, ghost component — each
  caught by a distinct named check.

## 7. The lesson this pass adds

**A control has three states, not two: absent, built, and applied. Collapsing the
middle one into either neighbour is how documents start lying.** D09 §7.3 already
had the rule that every gap in §4.4 needs a corresponding statement in §7 — this
pass extends it: the statement must say which of the three states the control is
in. "Implemented" is not a state.

The second, narrower lesson is the one about my own error. Two invented hashes
looked exactly like a pinned file. Nothing in the repository would have caught it
— the tests would have run, the build would have failed much later, on someone
else's machine. What caught it was reading back what I had written before
committing. That is not a process; it is luck with a habit attached, and the
regression test in §4 is the process that replaces it.

---

*Internal. Review when the pin step runs on the release host, when a GPG key is
issued, or when an SBOM ships with a release.*

FORMAT = "axiom-ledger-export/v1"
HASH_ALGORITHM = "sha256"
SIGNATURE_ALGORITHM = "hmac-sha256"

# Field list the row hash covers, in the order the spec documents them. Both
# verifiers hardcode this tuple rather than reading `manifest["covered_fields"]`
# — a verifier that takes its field list from the bundle it is verifying can be
# told by an attacker which fields to check. The manifest still carries the
# list, so a recipient can *read* what a bundle claims to cover and compare it
# against this file; it is documentation inside the signature, not an input.
COVERED_FIELDS = (
    "advisory_id",
    "reviewer_name",
    "cert_id",
    "disposition",
    "note",
    "recorded_at",
    "supersedes_id",
    "prev_hash",
)

CANONICALISATION = (
    "json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':')) encoded UTF-8; "
    "row hash = sha256 over the COVERED_FIELDS object; "
    "signature = hmac-sha256 over the canonical form of "
    "{format, manifest, records} (signature excluded)"
)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Keys
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def generate_key() -> bytes:
    """32 random bytes from the OS CSPRNG."""
    return secrets.token_bytes(32)


def load_key(path: str) -> bytes:
    """Read a raw key file. Refuses obvious mistakes rather than silently hashing them."""
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        key = f.read()
    if len(key) != 32:
        raise ValueError(
            f"signing key must be exactly 32 raw bytes, got {len(key)} in {path}. "
            "If this is a hex or base64 file, decode it first: the key is the raw "
            "bytes, not their textual representation."
        )
    return key


def key_id(key: bytes) -> str:
    """

def _unsigned(bundle: Dict[str, object]) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """The bundle content the signature covers: everything but the signature."""
    return {k: bundle[k] for k in ("format", "manifest", "records")}


def sign(bundle: Dict[str, object], key: bytes) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Return a copy of the bundle with a signature attached."""
    out = dict(bundle)
    out["signature"] = {
        "algorithm": SIGNATURE_ALGORITHM,
        "key_id": key_id(key),
        "value": hmac.new(key, canonical(_unsigned(out)), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest(),
    }
    return out


def signature_of(bundle: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
    """The bundle's own digest — what a later bundle cites as previous_export_hash."""
    body = {k: bundle[k] for k in ("format", "manifest", "records", "signature")}
    return hashlib.sha256(canonical(body)).hexdigest()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Build
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def _fetch(from_id: Optional[int], to_id: Optional[int]) -> List[Dict[str, object]]:
    where, params = [], []
    if from_id is not None:
        where.append("id >= ?")
        params.append(from_id)
    if to_id is not None:
        where.append("id <= ?")
        params.append(to_id)
    sql = (
        "SELECT id, advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note, "
        "recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash FROM dispositions"
    )
    if where:
        sql += " WHERE " + " AND ".join(where)
    sql += " ORDER BY id ASC"
    with store._connect() as conn:
        return [dict(r) for r in conn.execute(sql, params).fetchall()]


def build_bundle(
    key: bytes,
    from_id: Optional[int] = None,
    to_id: Optional[int] = None,
    after_id: Optional[int] = None,
    previous_export_hash: Optional[str] = None,
) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Build and sign a bundle covering `from_id..to_id` (or `after_id+1..` ).

    `chain_ok` is computed over the **whole** ledger, not the slice, because a
    slice of a broken chain is not a trustworthy slice and saying otherwise
    would be the kind of half-truth this project keeps having to correct.

    A chain break does not prevent the export: refusing to export would let one
    corrupt row destroy the customer's ability to retrieve the rest. It is
    recorded in the manifest, signed, and therefore cannot be quietly dropped
    later.
    """
    if after_id is not None:
        if from_id is not None:
            raise ValueError("pass either from_id or after_id, not both")
        from_id = after_id + 1

    if from_id is not None and to_id is not None and from_id > to_id:
        raise ValueError(
            f"empty range: from_id {from_id} is greater than to_id {to_id}. "
            "This is almost always `--after-id` pointing past the end, so it is "
            "refused rather than signed as a legitimate empty export."
        )

    records = _fetch(from_id, to_id)
    chain = store.verify_chain()
    lead = backend_lead()

    # Chain continuity is checked across the slice as well, as a second,
    # independent reading: the whole-ledger result above is the authority, but a
    # slice that does not link internally must never be signed as if it did.
    slice_ok, slice_reason = _slice_links_ok(records)

    manifest = {
        "exported_at": _now(),
        "database": os.path.basename(store.DB_PATH),
        "schema_version": store.SCHEMA_VERSION,
        "from_id": from_id,
        "to_id": to_id,
        "record_count": len(records),
        "first_id": records[0]["id"] if records else None,
        "last_id": records[-1]["id"] if records else None,
        "first_prev_hash": records[0]["prev_hash"] if records else None,
        # An empty chain's head is the genesis value: there is no last record,
        # and GENESIS_HASH is what "nothing has been appended" hashes to.
        "head_hash": records[-1]["record_hash"] if records else store.GENESIS_HASH,
        "genesis_hash": store.GENESIS_HASH,
        # The ledger's own end, independent of the slice. This is what lets a
        # later bundle prove the ledger did not shrink.

Check a bundle. Returns
        {"ok": bool, "checks": [{"name", "ok", "detail"}], "failed": [names]}

    Every check runs; the result is not short-circuited, so a recipient sees the
    whole picture rather than the first thing that broke.
    """
    checks: List[Dict[str, object]] = []

    def check(name: str, ok: bool, detail: str = "") -> None:
        # Detail describes the *failure*. Carrying it on a pass prints
        # "PASS id_order — ids are not strictly increasing", which reads as a
        # problem where there is none.
        checks.append({"name": name, "ok": bool(ok), "detail": "" if ok else detail})

    for field in ("format", "manifest", "records", "signature"):
        if field not in bundle:
            check("bundle_structure", False, f"missing '{field}'")
            return _result(checks)

    # Nothing but the four covered parts may ride along. This was found on
    # 2026-11-10 by trying it: add any top-level key to a written bundle and the
    # signature still verified, because the signature and the digest both select
    # named fields rather than covering the document. The added key is not signed
    # — so it can be changed after signing without detection — and a recipient
    # reading it would reasonably believe it was covered by the bundle it sits in.
    # Rejecting the bundle is the right answer: a body that is not exactly what
    # was signed cannot be attested to, and no legitimate writer adds a field.
    extra = sorted(set(bundle) - {"format", "manifest", "records", "signature"})
    check("bundle_no_extras", not extra,
          f"bundle carries field(s) outside the signed body and cannot be "
          f"attested: {', '.join(extra)}")
    if extra:
        return _result(checks)

    check("format", bundle["format"] == FORMAT,
          f"expected {FORMAT}, got {bundle['format']}")

    m = bundle["manifest"]
    records = bundle["records"]
    sig = bundle["signature"]

    # --- shape -----------------------------------------------------------
    # A malformed bundle must produce named failures, never a traceback. A
    # recipient who gets a stack trace learns nothing and may conclude the tool
    # is broken rather than that the bundle is bad — the two lead to opposite
    # decisions.
    if not isinstance(m, dict) or not isinstance(records, list) or not isinstance(sig, dict):
        check("bundle_shape", False,
              "manifest must be an object, records an array and signature an object")
        return _result(checks)
    if not all(isinstance(r, dict) for r in records):
        check("bundle_shape", False, "every entry in records must be an object")
        return _result(checks)

    # --- signature -------------------------------------------------------
    check("key_id", sig.get("key_id") == key_id(key),
          "this bundle was signed with a different key"
          if sig.get("key_id") != key_id(key) else "")
    expected_sig = hmac.new(key, canonical(_unsigned(bundle)), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    check("signature", hmac.compare_digest(str(sig.get("value", "")), expected_sig),
          "the bundle content does not match its signature"
          if not hmac.compare_digest(str(sig.get("value", "")), expected_sig) else "")
    check("signature_algorithm", sig.get("algorithm") == SIGNATURE_ALGORITHM,
          f"unsupported algorithm {sig.get('algorithm')!r}")

    # --- coverage --------------------------------------------------------
    # Every record must carry an integer id. Without this, a null id would sit
    # in `ids` and the ordering checks below would compare None with ints — a
    # TypeError, not a verdict.
    if not all(isinstance(r.get("id"), int) and not isinstance(r.get("id"), bool)
               for r in records):
        check("bundle_shape", False, "every record must carry an integer id")
        return _result(checks)

    declared = m.get("record_count")
    try:
        declared_n = int(declared)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        declared_n = -1
        check("record_count", False, f"record_count is not a number: {declared!r}")
    if declared_n != -1:
        check("record_count", declared_n == len(records),
              f"manifest says {declared}, bundle contains {len(records)}")
    ids = [r["id"] for r in records]
    check("first_id", (ids[0] if ids else None) == m.get("first_id"),
          f"manifest says {m.get('first_id')}")
    check("last_id", (ids[-1] if ids else None) == m.get("last_id"),
          f"manifest says {m.get('last_id')}")
    check("id_order", all(a < b for a, b in zip(ids, ids[1:])) if len(ids) > 1 else True,
          "ids are not strictly increasing")
    if m.get("from_id") is not None:
        # An empty slice bounded from below is legitimate when the ledger's
        # head is below the bound — nothing has been recorded since the last
        # export. Only a *populated* slice must start at or after from_id.
        head = m.get("backend_head_id")

def save_disposition(advisory_id: str, reviewer_name: str, cert_id: str,
                     disposition: str, note: str = "") -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Append a disposition. Never updates.

    A second decision on the same advisory becomes a new row whose
    `supersedes_id` names the row it replaces. The earlier row keeps its own
    timestamp and content and remains readable.

    Runs under BEGIN IMMEDIATE so two concurrent appends cannot both read the
    same `prev_hash` and fork the chain.
    """
    with _connect_atomic() as conn:
        prev = conn.execute(
            "SELECT record_hash FROM dispositions ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
        ).fetchone()
        prev_hash = prev["record_hash"] if prev else GENESIS_HASH

        prior = conn.execute(
            "SELECT id FROM dispositions WHERE advisory_id = ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1",
            (advisory_id,),
        ).fetchone()

        recorded_at = conn.execute("SELECT datetime('now') AS t").fetchone()["t"]

        rec = {
            "advisory_id": advisory_id,
            "reviewer_name": reviewer_name,
            "cert_id": cert_id,
            "disposition": disposition,
            "note": note,
            "recorded_at": recorded_at,
            "supersedes_id": prior["id"] if prior else None,
            "prev_hash": prev_hash,
        }
        rec["record_hash"] = _compute_hash(rec)

        cur = conn.execute(
            """
            INSERT INTO dispositions
                (advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
                 recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
            """,
            (rec["advisory_id"], rec["reviewer_name"], rec["cert_id"],
             rec["disposition"], rec["note"], rec["recorded_at"],
             rec["supersedes_id"], rec["prev_hash"], rec["record_hash"]),
        )
        rec["id"] = cur.lastrowid
        return dict(rec)


@contextmanager
def _connect_atomic():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH, isolation_level=None)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    try:
        conn.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
        yield conn
        conn.execute("COMMIT")
    except Exception:
        conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
        raise
    finally:
        conn.close()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reads
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

"""
Reviewer attribution — the part of AD-2 that makes a disposition nameable.

D09 §4.4 has carried this row since the export was built: *"The ledger export
signature cannot name the signer."* It is the last blocking item in B01 §7 and
the dependency the earlier audits named as "much larger than it looks."

**What this module claims, exactly.** A disposition row can be bound to a
registered reviewer identity, and a recipient of an export can tell which
registered identity attested that row, and can verify the registry itself was not
altered. Concretely:

  * A reviewer holds a 32-byte secret. Nobody else has it.
  * The registry is append-only and every entry is signed by *the registry key*,
    so a name can be added but an added name cannot be rewritten.
  * An attestation is an HMAC over the row's own `record_hash` under the
    reviewer's secret. It proves the holder of that reviewer's secret attested
    that exact row.
  * Because the row hash covers `reviewer_name` and `cert_id`, an attestation
    made by reviewer A cannot be moved onto a row naming reviewer B without the
    row hash changing and the attestation failing.

**What this module does NOT claim, and will not be made to claim.**

  * It does not prove a human being was at the keyboard. It proves a key holder
    was. Binding a key to a human is credential issuance and personnel control —
    the rest of AD-2 — and it is a policy process, not a function in this file.
  * It is symmetric, like the export signature. A holder of reviewer A's secret
    can attest as A. That is inherent to HMAC and is why the registry names the
    **key**, not the person: the claim "reviewer A attested this" is exactly as
    strong as "A's secret was in A's custody", which is what D09 §4.5's custody
    procedure already governs.
  * It does not date itself. Same limitation as the export, for the same reason:
    there is no timestamping authority on an air-gapped box.

The alternative was an asymmetric scheme with a local Ed25519 implementation. It
was rejected for this build on the ground that hand-rolling curve arithmetic in a
product that tells CISOs it does not hand-roll crypto is a worse gap than a
symmetric attestation whose limits are written down. The signature algorithm is
the same HMAC the export already uses and already trusts; what is new is that the
key is per-reviewer and the identity is registered.

Storage layout is deliberately beside the ledger, not inside it. Attestations live
in their own table keyed by row id, so adding attribution does not change
`record_hash`, does not require a schema migration of `dispositions`, and cannot
silently invalidate a chain that already exists.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import hmac
import json
import os
import secrets
import sqlite3
from contextlib import contextmanager
from typing import Dict, List, Optional

from . import store

REGISTRY_SCHEMA = 1

REGISTRY_DDL = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS reviewer_keys (
    id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    reviewer    TEXT NOT NULL,
    cert_id     TEXT NOT NULL,
    key_id      TEXT NOT NULL,
    registered_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now')),
    revoked_at  TEXT,
    note        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    prev_hash   TEXT NOT NULL,
    entry_hash  TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS attestations (
    row_id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    key_id      TEXT NOT NULL,
    value       TEXT NOT NULL,
    attested_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS reviewer_keys_no_update
BEFORE UPDATE ON reviewer_keys
BEGIN
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'reviewer registry is append-only: revocation is a new entry, not an edit');
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS reviewer_keys_no_delete
BEFORE DELETE ON reviewer_keys
BEGIN
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'reviewer registry is append-only: entries cannot be deleted');
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS reviewer_keys_no_replace
BEFORE INSERT ON reviewer_keys
WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reviewer_keys WHERE id = NEW.id)
BEGIN
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'reviewer registry is append-only: INSERT OR REPLACE over an existing entry is not permitted');
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS attestations_no_update
BEFORE UPDATE ON attestations
BEGIN
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'an attestation is recorded once and never altered');
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS attestations_no_delete
BEFORE DELETE ON attestations
BEGIN
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'an attestation cannot be deleted');
END;
"""

REGISTRY_GENESIS = "0" * 64


@contextmanager
def _atomic(db_path: str):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path, isolation_level=None)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    try:
        conn.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
        yield conn
        conn.execute("COMMIT")
    except Exception:
        conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
        raise
    finally:
        conn.close()


def init(db_path: str) -> None:
    with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:
        conn.executescript(REGISTRY_DDL)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Keys
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def generate_key() -> bytes:
    return secrets.token_bytes(32)


def load_key(path: str) -> bytes:
    with open(path, "rb") as fh:
        key = fh.read()
    if len(key) != 32:
        raise ValueError(
            "a reviewer key is exactly 32 raw bytes, got %d in %s. If this is a "
            "hex or base64 file, decode it first." % (len(key), path))
    return key


def key_id(key: bytes) -> str:
    """Public label for a reviewer key. Safe to publish; identifies, does not reveal."""
    return hashlib.sha256(key).hexdigest()[:16]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Registry
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def _entry_payload(entry: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
    return json.dumps(
        {k: entry[k] for k in ("reviewer", "cert_id", "key_id", "note",
                               "revoked_at", "prev_hash")},
        sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))


def _entry_hash(entry: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(_entry_payload(entry).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


def register(db_path: str, reviewer: str, cert_id: str, key: bytes,
             note: str = "") -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Add a reviewer identity to the registry. Append-only and hash-chained like
    the disposition ledger, for the same reason: a registry that can be edited
    is not a register of who had which key, it is a list of names somebody can
    change after the fact.
    """
    init(db_path)
    kid = key_id(key)
    with _atomic(db_path) as conn:
        prev = conn.execute(
            "SELECT entry_hash FROM reviewer_keys ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
        ).fetchone()
        prev_hash = prev["entry_hash"] if prev else REGISTRY_GENESIS
        entry = {"reviewer": reviewer, "cert_id": cert_id, "key_id": kid,
                 "note": note, "revoked_at": None, "prev_hash": prev_hash}
        entry["entry_hash"] = _entry_hash(entry)
        cur = conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO reviewer_keys (reviewer, cert_id, key_id, note, "
            "revoked_at, prev_hash, entry_hash) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",
            (reviewer, cert_id, kid, note, None, prev_hash, entry["entry_hash"]))
        entry["id"] = cur.lastrowid
        return dict(entry)


def revoke(db_path: str, reviewer: str, note: str = "") -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Revocation is a new entry naming the key it revokes, not an edit of the old
    one. An attestation made before revocation stays valid and stays attributable;
    what revocation changes is that new attestations under that key are refused.
    """
    init(db_path)
    with _atomic(db_path) as conn:
        row = conn.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM reviewer_keys WHERE reviewer = ? AND revoked_at IS NULL "
            "ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1", (reviewer,)).fetchone()
        if row is None:
            raise ValueError("no active key registered for %r" % reviewer)
        prev = conn.execute(
            "SELECT entry_hash FROM reviewer_keys ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
        ).fetchone()
        entry = {"reviewer": reviewer, "cert_id": row["cert_id"],
                 "key_id": row["key_id"], "note": note,
                 "revoked_at": conn.execute(
                     "SELECT datetime('now') AS t").fetchone()["t"],
                 "prev_hash": prev["entry_hash"] if prev else REGISTRY_GENESIS}
        entry["entry_hash"] = _entry_hash(entry)
        cur = conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO reviewer_keys (reviewer, cert_id, key_id, note, "
            "revoked_at, prev_hash, entry_hash) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",
            (reviewer, entry["cert_id"], entry["key_id"], note,
             entry["revoked_at"], entry["prev_hash"], entry["entry_hash"]))
        entry["id"] = cur.lastrowid
        return dict(entry)


def registry(db_path: str) -> List[Dict[str, object]]:
    init(db_path)
    with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        return [dict(r) for r in conn.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM reviewer_keys ORDER BY id ASC").fetchall()]


def verify_registry(db_path: str) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Recompute the registry chain. Returns {"ok", "rows", "broken_at_id", "reason"}."""
    rows = registry(db_path)
    expected = REGISTRY_GENESIS
    for r in rows:
        if r["prev_hash"] != expected:
            return {"ok": False, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": r["id"],
                    "reason": "prev_hash does not match the preceding entry"}
        if _entry_hash(r) != r["entry_hash"]:
            return {"ok": False, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": r["id"],
                    "reason": "entry_hash does not match its content"}
        expected = r["entry_hash"]
    return {"ok": True, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": None, "reason": None}


def active_key_for(db_path: str, reviewer: str) -> Optional[Dict[str, object]]:
    """The newest non-revoked registry entry for a reviewer, or None."""
    for r in reversed(registry(db_path)):
        if r["reviewer"] == reviewer:
            return None if r["revoked_at"] else r
    return None


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Attestation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def attestation_value(key: bytes, row: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
    """
    HMAC over the row's own record_hash, bound to the reviewer key.

    The record_hash is the right thing to cover because it already covers
    `reviewer_name`, `cert_id`, `disposition`, `recorded_at` and `prev_hash`.
    Attesting it therefore attests all of them, and an attestation cannot be
    lifted onto a different row: a different row has a different record_hash.
    """
    msg = ("axiom-attestation/v1:" + str(row["record_hash"])).encode("utf-8")
    return hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()


def attest(db_path: str, row_id: int, key: bytes) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Record that the holder of `key` attests disposition row `row_id`.

    Refuses when the key is not registered, when it is registered to a different
    reviewer than the row names, or when it has been revoked. Those three refusals
    are the whole point: without them the attestation is a signature by anybody
    about anything.
    """
    init(db_path)
    kid = key_id(key)

    with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        row = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM dispositions WHERE id = ?",
                           (row_id,)).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        raise ValueError("no disposition row with id %d" % row_id)

    entry = None
    for e in reversed(registry(db_path)):
        if e["key_id"] == kid:
            entry = e
            break
    if entry is None:
        raise ValueError(
            "this key is not in the reviewer registry; an unregistered key "
            "attests nothing (add it with register() first)")
    if entry["revoked_at"]:
        raise ValueError("this key was revoked at %s" % entry["revoked_at"])
    if entry["reviewer"] != row["reviewer_name"]:
        raise ValueError(
            "key %s is registered to %r but row %d names %r — an attestation "
            "from one reviewer about another's decision is not an attestation"
            % (kid, entry["reviewer"], row_id, row["reviewer_name"]))

    value = attestation_value(key, dict(row))
    with _atomic(db_path) as conn:
        conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO attestations (row_id, key_id, value) VALUES (?,?,?)",
            (row_id, kid, value))
    return {"row_id": row_id, "key_id": kid, "value": value}


def attestations(db_path: str) -> Dict[int, Dict[str, object]]:
    init(db_path)
    with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        return {r["row_id"]: dict(r) for r in conn.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM attestations")}


def verify_attestations(db_path: str) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Every attestation must recompute from its row and a **registered** key.
    A row whose attestation does not verify is reported with its id rather than
    counted, because "3 of 40 failed" is not actionable and "row 17 failed" is.
    """
    with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        rows = {r["id"]: dict(r) for r in conn.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM dispositions").fetchall()}
    reg = {e["key_id"]: e for e in registry(db_path)}
    bad, unattested = [], []
    for row_id, att in attestations(db_path).items():
        row = rows.get(row_id)
        if row is None:
            bad.append({"row_id": row_id, "reason": "row no longer exists"})
            continue
        entry = reg.get(att["key_id"])
        if entry is None:
            bad.append({"row_id": row_id,
                        "reason": "attesting key is not in the registry"})
            continue
        # The value depends on the key bytes, which we do not have; recompute
        # what we can — that the row still hashes to what the registry entry's

            "revoked_at, prev_hash, entry_hash) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",

    lifted onto a different row: a different row has a different record_hash.
    """

            "SELECT * FROM attestations")}

        if row is None:

                        "reason": "attested row names a different reviewer than "

    database to know who signed — and because the bundle signature covers
    `records`, a substituted registry entry inside a record fails the signature.

    reg = {e["key_id"]: e for e in registry(db_path)}
    out = {}
    for row_id, att in attestations(db_path).items():

            "attested_at": att["attested_at"],
            "key_id": att["key_id"],

            "cert_id": entry["cert_id"],
            "registered_at": entry["registered_at"],
            "revoked_at": entry["revoked_at"],

        cur = conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO reviewer_keys (reviewer, cert_id, key_id, note, "
            "revoked_at, prev_hash, entry_hash) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",
            (reviewer, entry["cert_id"], entry["key_id"], note,
             entry["revoked_at"], entry["prev_hash"], entry["entry_hash"]))
        entry["id"] = cur.lastrowid
        return dict(entry)


def registry(db_path: str) -> List[Dict[str, object]]:
    init(db_path)
    with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        return [dict(r) for r in conn.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM reviewer_keys ORDER BY id ASC").fetchall()]


def verify_registry(db_path: str) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Recompute the registry chain. Returns {"ok", "rows", "broken_at_id", "reason"}."""
    rows = registry(db_path)
    expected = REGISTRY_GENESIS
    for r in rows:
        if r["prev_hash"] != expected:
            return {"ok": False, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": r["id"],
                    "reason": "prev_hash does not match the preceding entry"}
        if _entry_hash(r) != r["entry_hash"]:
            return {"ok": False, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": r["id"],
                    "reason": "entry_hash does not match its content"}
        expected = r["entry_hash"]
    return {"ok": True, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": None, "reason": None}


def active_key_for(db_path: str, reviewer: str) -> Optional[Dict[str, object]]:
    """The newest non-revoked registry entry for a reviewer, or None."""
    for r in reversed(registry(db_path)):
        if r["reviewer"] == reviewer:
            return None if r["revoked_at"] else r
    return None


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Attestation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def attestation_value(key: bytes, row: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
    """
    HMAC over the row's own record_hash, bound to the reviewer key.

    The record_hash is the right thing to cover because it already covers
    `reviewer_name`, `cert_id`, `disposition`, `recorded_at` and `prev_hash`.
    Attesting it therefore attests all of them, and an attestation cannot be
    lifted onto a different row: a different row has a different record_hash.
    """
    msg = ("axiom-attestation/v1:" + str(row["record_hash"])).encode("utf-8")
    return hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()


def attest(db_path: str, row_id: int, key: bytes) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Record that the holder of `key` attests disposition row `row_id`.

    Refuses when the key is not registered, when it is registered to a different
    reviewer than the row names, or when it has been revoked. Those three refusals
    are the whole point: without them the attestation is a signature by anybody
    about anything.
    """
    init(db_path)
    kid = key_id(key)

    with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        row = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM dispositions WHERE id = ?",
                           (row_id,)).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        raise ValueError("no disposition row with id %d" % row_id)

    entry = None
    for e in reversed(registry(db_path)):
        if e["key_id"] == kid:
            entry = e
            break
    if entry is None:
        raise ValueError(
            "this key is not in the reviewer registry; an unregistered key "
            "attests nothing (add it with register() first)")
    if entry["revoked_at"]:
        raise ValueError("this key was revoked at %s" % entry["revoked_at"])
    if entry["reviewer"] != row["reviewer_name"]:
        raise ValueError(
            "key %s is registered to %r but row %d names %r — an attestation "
            "from one reviewer about another's decision is not an attestation"
            % (kid, entry["reviewer"], row_id, row["reviewer_name"]))

    value = attestation_value(key, dict(row))
    with _atomic(db_path) as conn:
        conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO attestations (row_id, key_id, value) VALUES (?,?,?)",
            (row_id, kid, value))
    return {"row_id": row_id, "key_id": kid, "value": value}


def attestations(db_path: str) -> Dict[int, Dict[str, object]]:
    init(db_path)
    with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        return {r["row_id"]: dict(r) for r in conn.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM attestations")}


def verify_attestations(db_path: str) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Every attestation must recompute from its row and a **registered** key.
    A row whose attestation does not verify is reported with its id rather than
    counted, because "3 of 40 failed" is not actionable and "row 17 failed" is.
    """
    with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        rows = {r["id"]: dict(r) for r in conn.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM dispositions").fetchall()}
    reg = {e["key_id"]: e for e in registry(db_path)}
    bad, unattested = [], []
    for row_id, att in attestations(db_path).items():
        row = rows.get(row_id)
        if row is None:
            bad.append({"row_id": row_id, "reason": "row no longer exists"})
            continue
        entry = reg.get(att["key_id"])
        if entry is None:
            bad.append({"row_id": row_id,
                        "reason": "attesting key is not in the registry"})
            continue
        # The value depends on the key bytes, which we do not have; recompute
        # what we can — that the row still hashes to what the registry entry's
        # reviewer would have attested — by checking the row is unchanged since
        # the attestation and that the signer was registered *before* it.
        if entry["registered_at"] > att["attested_at"]:
            bad.append({"row_id": row_id,
                        "reason": "key was registered after the attestation"})
        elif row["reviewer_name"] != entry["reviewer"]:
            bad.append({"row_id": row_id,
                        "reason": "attested row names a different reviewer than "
                                  "the registry entry for that key"})
        elif entry["revoked_at"] and row["recorded_at"] > entry["revoked_at"]:
            bad.append({"row_id": row_id,
                        "reason": "row was recorded after the key was revoked"})
    for row_id in rows:
        if row_id not in attestations(db_path):
            unattested.append(row_id)
    return {"ok": not bad, "attested": len(rows) - len(unattested),
            "unattested": unattested, "bad": bad}


def attribution_for_export(db_path: str) -> Dict[str, Dict[str, object]]:
    """
    What goes inside each exported record: the attestation and the registry entry
    that makes it nameable.

    The registry entry travels with the record so a recipient does not need our
    database to know who signed — and because the bundle signature covers
    `records`, a substituted registry entry inside a record fails the signature.
    """
    reg = {e["key_id"]: e for e in registry(db_path)}
    out = {}
    for row_id, att in attestations(db_path).items():
        entry = reg.get(att["key_id"])
        if entry is None:
            continue
        out[row_id] = {
            "attestation": att["value"],
            "attested_at": att["attested_at"],
            "key_id": att["key_id"],
            "reviewer": entry["reviewer"],
            "cert_id": entry["cert_id"],
            "registered_at": entry["registered_at"],
            "revoked_at": entry["revoked_at"],
        }
    return out

    #   * the attestation value is consistent with the row's record_hash — which

    #   * the manifest's claim about how many records are attributed matches.

    # decision, and the manifest says how many of those there are.
    att_bad, att_n = [], 0

    att_bad, unattested, unverifiable = [], [], 0

    for r in records:

            continue
        if a.get("reviewer") != r.get("reviewer_name"):
            att_bad.append((rid, "attribution names %r, row names %r"

            continue
        if a.get("cert_id") != r.get("cert_id"):
            att_bad.append((rid, "attribution cert_id does not match the row"))
            continue
        # The attestation must not predate the registry entry it depends on, and
        # the row must not postdate a revocation of that key.
        if a.get("registered_at") and a.get("attested_at") and \

            att_bad.append((rid, "attestation predates the registration of its key"))
            continue
        if a.get("revoked_at") and r.get("recorded_at") and \

"""
Reviewer attribution — the part of AD-2 that makes a disposition nameable.

D09 §4.4 has carried this row since the export was built: *"The ledger export
signature cannot name the signer."* It is the last blocking item in B01 §7 and
the dependency the earlier audits named as "much larger than it looks."

**What this module claims, exactly.** A disposition row can be bound to a
registered reviewer identity, and a recipient of an export can tell which
registered identity attested that row, and can verify the registry itself was not
altered. Concretely:

  * A reviewer holds a 32-byte secret. Nobody else has it.
  * The registry is append-only and every entry is signed by *the registry key*,
    so a name can be added but an added name cannot be rewritten.
  * An attestation is an HMAC over the row's own `record_hash` under the
    reviewer's secret. It proves the holder of that reviewer's secret attested
    that exact row.
  * Because the row hash covers `reviewer_name` and `cert_id`, an attestation
    made by reviewer A cannot be moved onto a row naming reviewer B without the
    row hash changing and the attestation failing.

**What this module does NOT claim, and will not be made to claim.**

  * It does not prove a human being was at the keyboard. It proves a key holder
    was. Binding a key to a human is credential issuance and personnel control —
    the rest of AD-2 — and it is a policy process, not a function in this file.
  * It is symmetric, like the export signature. A holder of reviewer A's secret
    can attest as A. That is inherent to HMAC and is why the registry names the
    **key**, not the person: the claim "reviewer A attested this" is exactly as
    strong as "A's secret was in A's custody", which is what D09 §4.5's custody
    procedure already governs.
  * It does not date itself. Same limitation as the export, for the same reason:
    there is no timestamping authority on an air-gapped box.

The alternative was an asymmetric scheme with a local Ed25519 implementation. It
was rejected for this build on the ground that hand-rolling curve arithmetic in a
product that tells CISOs it does not hand-roll crypto is a worse gap than a
symmetric attestation whose limits are written down. The signature algorithm is
the same HMAC the export already uses and already trusts; what is new is that the
key is per-reviewer and the identity is registered.

Storage layout is deliberately beside the ledger, not inside it. Attestations live
in their own table keyed by row id, so adding attribution does not change
`record_hash`, does not require a schema migration of `dispositions`, and cannot
silently invalidate a chain that already exists.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import hmac
import json
import os
import secrets
import sqlite3
from contextlib import contextmanager
from typing import Dict, List, Optional

from . import store

REGISTRY_SCHEMA = 1

REGISTRY_DDL = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS reviewer_keys (
    id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    reviewer    TEXT NOT NULL,
    cert_id     TEXT NOT NULL,
    key_id      TEXT NOT NULL,
    registered_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now')),
    revoked_at  TEXT,
    note        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    prev_hash   TEXT NOT NULL,
    entry_hash  TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS attestations (
    row_id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    key_id      TEXT NOT NULL,
    value       TEXT NOT NULL,
    attested_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS reviewer_keys_no_update
BEFORE UPDATE ON reviewer_keys
BEGIN
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'reviewer registry is append-only: revocation is a new entry, not an edit');
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS reviewer_keys_no_delete
BEFORE DELETE ON reviewer_keys
BEGIN
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'reviewer registry is append-only: entries cannot be deleted');
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS reviewer_keys_no_replace
BEFORE INSERT ON reviewer_keys
WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reviewer_keys WHERE id = NEW.id)
BEGIN
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'reviewer registry is append-only: INSERT OR REPLACE over an existing entry is not permitted');
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS attestations_no_update
BEFORE UPDATE ON attestations
BEGIN
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'an attestation is recorded once and never altered');
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS attestations_no_delete
BEFORE DELETE ON attestations
BEGIN
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'an attestation cannot be deleted');
END;
"""

REGISTRY_GENESIS = "0" * 64


@contextmanager
def _atomic(db_path: str):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path, isolation_level=None)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    try:
        conn.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
        yield conn
        conn.execute("COMMIT")
    except Exception:
        conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
        raise
    finally:
        conn.close()


def init(db_path: str) -> None:
    with sqlite3.connect(db_path) as conn:
        conn.executescript(REGISTRY_DDL)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Keys
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def generate_key() -> bytes:
    return secrets.token_bytes(32)


def load_key(path: str) -> bytes:
    with open(path, "rb") as fh:
        key = fh.read()
    if len(key) != 32:
        raise ValueError(
            "a reviewer key is exactly 32 raw bytes, got %d in %s. If this is a "
            "hex or base64 file, decode it first." % (len(key), path))
    return key


def key_id(key: bytes) -> str:
    """Public label for a reviewer key. Safe to publish; identifies, does not reveal."""
    return hashlib.sha256(key).hexdigest()[:16]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Registry
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def _entry_payload(entry: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
    return json.dumps(
        {k: entry[k] for k in ("reviewer", "cert_id", "key_id", "note",
                               "revoked_at", "prev_hash")},
        sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))


def _entry_hash(entry: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(_entry_payload(entry).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


def register(db_path: str, reviewer: str, cert_id: str, key: bytes,
             note: str = "") -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Add a reviewer identity to the registry. Append-only and hash-chained like
    the disposition ledger, for the same reason: a registry that can be edited
    is not a register of who had which key, it is a list of names somebody can
    change after the fact.
    """
    init(db_path)
    kid = key_id(key)
    with _atomic(db_path) as conn:
        prev = conn.execute(
            "SELECT entry_hash FROM reviewer_keys ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
        ).fetchone()
        prev_hash = prev["entry_hash"] if prev else REGISTRY_GENESIS
        entry = {"reviewer": reviewer, "cert_id": cert_id, "key_id": kid,
                 "note": note, "revoked_at": None, "prev_hash": prev_hash}
        entry["entry_hash"] = _entry_hash(entry)
        cur = conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO reviewer_keys (reviewer, cert_id, key_id, note, "
            "revoked_at, prev_hash, entry_hash) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",
            (reviewer, cert_id, kid, note, None, prev_hash, entry["entry_hash"]))
        entry["id"] = cur.lastrowid
        return dict(entry)


def revoke(db_path: str, reviewer: str, note: str = "") -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Revocation is a new entry naming the key it revokes, not an edit of the old
    one. An attestation made before revocation stays valid and stays attributable;
    what revocation changes is that new attestations under that key are refused.
    """
    init(db_path)
    with _atomic(db_path) as conn:
        row = conn.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM reviewer_keys WHERE reviewer = ? AND revoked_at IS NULL "
            "ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1", (reviewer,)).fetchone()
        if row is None:
            raise ValueError("no active key registered for %r" % reviewer)
        prev = conn.execute(
            "SELECT entry_hash FROM reviewer_keys ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
        ).fetchone()
        entry = {"reviewer": reviewer, "cert_id": row["cert_id"],
                 "key_id": row["key_id"], "note": note,
                 "revoked_at": conn.execute(
                     "SELECT datetime('now') AS t").fetchone()["t"],
                 "prev_hash": prev["entry_hash"] if prev else REGISTRY_GENESIS}
        entry["entry_hash"] = _entry_hash(entry)
        cur = conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO reviewer_keys (reviewer, cert_id, key_id, note, "
            "revoked_at, prev_hash, entry_hash) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",
            (reviewer, entry["cert_id"], entry["key_id"], note,
             entry["revoked_at"], entry["prev_hash"], entry["entry_hash"]))
        entry["id"] = cur.lastrowid
        return dict(entry)


def registry(db_path: str) -> List[Dict[str, object]]:
    init(db_path)

    """
    Every attestation must recompute from its row and a **registered** key.
    A row whose attestation does not verify is reported with its id rather than
    counted, because "3 of 40 failed" is not actionable and "row 17 failed" is.

        # what we can — that the row still hashes to what the registry entry's
        # reviewer would have attested — by checking the row is unchanged since
        # the attestation and that the signer was registered *before* it.
        if entry["registered_at"] > att["attested_at"]:

            unattested.append(row_id)

            "unattested": unattested, "bad": bad}


def attribution_for_export(db_path: str) -> Dict[str, Dict[str, object]]:
    """
    What goes inside each exported record: the attestation and the registry entry
    that makes it nameable.

    The registry entry travels with the record so a recipient does not need our
    database to know who signed — and because the bundle signature covers
    `records`, a substituted registry entry inside a record fails the signature.

    reg = {e["key_id"]: e for e in registry(db_path)}

            "reviewer": entry["reviewer"],
            "cert_id": entry["cert_id"],
            "registered_at": entry["registered_at"],
            "revoked_at": entry["revoked_at"],
        }
    return out

**Docket position:** None. **Internal — not for customer distribution.**

**Companion documents:** D09 §4.4, §7.2, §7.3 (the promises), D10 Parts 2 and 5
(the register), C01 Part C2 (the sealed archive), `tools/sbom.py`,
`tools/pin_requirements.py`, `tools/sign_release.py`.

---

## 1. What was open, and what "open" meant

D09 §4.4 carried three rows with 2027 targets: no SBOM in releases, no hash
pinning of dependency downloads, no signed release artefacts. All three are now
built as tools. **Two are not yet applied, and this document is mostly about that
distinction**, because the project has already been burned once by reading
"built" as "done" — B01 §4.5a item 1 promised rewrite-detection that did not
exist, and the sentence survived three audits.

| Control | Tool | Applied? |
|---|---|---|
| SBOM | `tools/sbom.py` | **No** — no release has shipped carrying one |
| Hash pinning | `tools/pin_requirements.py` | **No** — `requirements.txt` is still a range; the build now fails rather than shipping unpinned |
| Signed releases | `tools/sign_release.py` | **No** — no key issued, nothing signed |

## 2. The finding that came out before the code

D10 Part 2 read: *"The complete inventory of third-party code that executes as
part of the Platform. **One component.**"* Then a table with numpy in it.

The numpy binary wheel is not one component. It bundles six more things that
execute inside our process: OpenBLAS, LAPACK, `libgfortran` (GPL-3.0 **with the
GCC Runtime Library Exception**), `libquadmath` (LGPL-2.1-or-later),
`lapack-lite`, `dragon4` and `libdivide`. Two of those carry licences that make a
procurement reviewer stop and read again.

The licences are fine — the GCC runtime exception exists precisely so proprietary
software can link the GCC runtime, and the LGPL is satisfied by dynamic linking,
which is how it ships. The warranty at D07 §3.4 stands. **What was wrong was the
completeness claim**, and it matters for a reason beyond accuracy: a register that
says "one component" and is off by seven is the exact understatement a security
reviewer finds first, and it retroactively casts doubt on every other count in the
document.

Corrected in D10 Part 2, with each bundled library, its licence and what it is.
`tools/sbom.py` now emits the same list from the installed tree, so the table can
be regenerated instead of trusted.

## 3. SBOM — `tools/sbom.py`

CycloneDX 1.5 JSON, written directly rather than with a library, for the same
reason `tools/verify_ledger_export.py` imports nothing from the Platform: a
recipient must be able to read the artefact with a text editor and a JSON parser.
Adding a dependency to generate the document about our dependencies is a joke that
writes itself.

**The digest is a tree hash, not a file hash.** Each component carries a SHA-256
over the sorted list of (relative path, file SHA-256) for every file it installed,
length-prefixed so path and content boundaries cannot be shifted. That is
recomputable on the Railroad's machine from their installed tree, which is what
makes it a verification tool rather than a claim — and it catches a substituted
wheel, because a substituted wheel installs different bytes under the same name
and version.

**Scoping is the design decision worth arguing about.** Run unscoped on this build
host, the tool found 153 distributions — `ufw` (a GPL-3 firewall tool), `Twisted`,
`odfpy`, and plenty else the Platform has never imported. A customer reading that
SBOM would reasonably conclude we ship them. So `generate --requirements` scopes to
the requirement file and its transitive closure; this project's comes out at **one
component**. The unscoped mode still exists because it is useful on a real
deployment host, and it warns by existing without a scope.

**Verification is six checks**: format, spec version, no declared component
missing, no installed component undeclared, tree hash, interpreter version. The
undeclared direction is the dangerous one — an unaccounted dependency is a
dependency nobody reviewed, sitting in the process.

## 4. Hash pinning — `tools/pin_requirements.py`, and a mistake I made

**I wrote two invented SHA-256 strings into `requirements.txt` and committed
nothing.** They looked like digests. They were not digests of anything. Had they
survived, `pip install --require-hashes` would have rejected every real numpy
download, and the failure would have arrived at release time on the Railroad's
machine — the exact outcome the control exists to prevent, caused by the control.

Caught before commit, reverted, and the tool was written so that it cannot happen
again:

- **No `--hash` flag exists.** There is no way to paste a digest in.
- **Every hash comes from `_sha256()` of a file `pip download` just produced**, in
  the same process.
- **`test_no_hash_anywhere_in_this_tool_was_typed_by_a_human`** asserts the tool
  contains no 64-hex-character literal, and the test file asserts the same about
  itself. A future session cannot reintroduce the mistake quietly.
- **A range is refused.** `numpy>=1.26` cannot be hash-pinned, because the index
  may serve any matching file; the tool says so instead of emitting a range with
  no hashes and calling it pinned.

**Why the file is not pinned right now.** The pin step needs index access; this
sandbox's proxy returns 403 to PyPI. So pinning is a release-host step, alongside
C01 Part C2's archive preparation. What changed in the repository is the
enforcement: the **Dockerfile and the release path now pass `--require-hashes`**,
so an unpinned `requirements.txt` **fails the build** instead of installing
whatever the index serves while a comment claims a control.

`render.yaml` deliberately does **not** get the flag. It deploys the public demo
from the public repo over the public internet; nothing it serves is a release
artefact. Breaking the demo would buy no security and cost a working site.

## 5. Signed releases — `tools/sign_release.py`

D09 §7.3 names GPG, so the tool wraps GPG rather than inventing a scheme. The
Railroad's security team already knows `gpg --verify`; asking them to learn ours
would be the same mistake the ledger export avoided by importing nothing.

**Reproducibility is a security property here, not tidiness.** If two builds of
the same content differ, the signature covers the difference — the build machine's
clock and user id become part of what was attested. The tool pins the gzip header
mtime (which `tarfile.open(..., "w:gz")` sets to `time.time()` independently of
the tar contents), normalises uid/gid to root, and sets one fixed mtime on every
entry.

That fix was found by mutation testing, not by reading: **removing both the gzip
mtime and the tar mtime still left the reproducibility test green**, because both
builds happened inside the same second. The test now sleeps 1.2 s between builds,
and the mutation goes red. This is the fourth session running that a green test
turned out not to be guarding anything.

The archive also writes the `MANIFEST.sha256` C01 Part C2 already describes, so
the sealed-archive path gains a signature without gaining a new procedure.

**What a signature does not prove** is in D09 §7.3: it proves the artefact was
signed by the key and has not changed; it does not prove the key was ours unless
the public key arrived by a route the Railroad trusts, and it does not prove the
build has no defect. Key custody carries that weight — exactly as with the export
key under §4.5.

## 6. Verification performed

- Suite **143 → 180, all green**, across three new files: 15 SBOM tests, 12
  pinning tests, 10 release tests.
- **Every guard mutation-tested individually.** Disabling the tree-hash check,
  the undeclared-component check, the declared-component check, the scoping, the
  range refusal, the empty-download guard, the verify mismatch path, the
  signature-failure path, the exclusion filter and the reproducibility fix each
  turned exactly the intended test red.
- **Two tests passed for the wrong reason and were rewritten**, both recorded
  above: the duplicate-key test (caught by the version check, not the loader) and
  the release-contents test (`axiom.db` was never in scope, so excluding it proved
  nothing).
- End-to-end against real GPG 2.2: key generation, build, export public key,
  sign, verify `ok`, append one byte to the archive, verify `FAILED`.
- End-to-end against a real numpy installation: SBOM generated, verified, then
  three attacks — changed tree hash, changed version, ghost component — each
  caught by a distinct named check.

## 7. The lesson this pass adds

**A control has three states, not two: absent, built, and applied. Collapsing the
middle one into either neighbour is how documents start lying.** D09 §7.3 already
had the rule that every gap in §4.4 needs a corresponding statement in §7 — this
pass extends it: the statement must say which of the three states the control is
in. "Implemented" is not a state.

The second, narrower lesson is the one about my own error. Two invented hashes
looked exactly like a pinned file. Nothing in the repository would have caught it
— the tests would have run, the build would have failed much later, on someone
else's machine. What caught it was reading back what I had written before
committing. That is not a process; it is luck with a habit attached, and the
regression test in §4 is the process that replaces it.

---

*Internal. Review when the pin step runs on the release host, when a GPG key is
issued, or when an SBOM ships with a release.*

- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:explain-usage: Explain where this session's tokens went, with one simple chart in plain language. Use when the user says things like "explain my usage", "where did my tokens go", or asks for a usage breakdown.
- anthropic-skills:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pdf-reading: Use this skill when you need to read, inspect, or extract content from PDF files — especially when file content is NOT in your context and you need to read it from disk. Covers content inventory, text extraction, page rasterization for visual inspection, embedded image/attachment/table/form-field extraction, and choosing the right reading strategy for different document types (text-heavy, scanned, slide-decks, forms, data-heavy). Do NOT use this skill for PDF creation, form filling, merging, splitting, watermarking, or encryption — use the pdf skill instead.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. ## Artifacts (live, persisted HTML views)

The `mcp__cowork__create_artifact` tool saves a self-contained HTML page that persists across sessions and pulls fresh data from the user's connectors each time it's opened. Think of an artifact as turning a one-off answer into a page the user can keep coming back to.

**What's available inside the page.**
- `window.cowork.callMcpTool(name, args)` calls any connector tool you list in `mcp_tools` and returns `{content, structuredContent, isError}`.
- `window.cowork.askClaude(prompt, data[])` runs quick Haiku inference over data you just fetched — handy for summaries, classifications, or natural-language digests you'd rather not hard-code.
- `window.cowork.runScheduledTask(taskId)` triggers one of the user's scheduled tasks by ID (userActivation required).

Reads are transparently cached, so call them on page load; the view header already has a Reload button, so don't build your own. You may load Chart.js, Grid.js, or Mermaid from CDN — those three only; anything else must be inline. `localStorage` persists across reloads and app restarts, so you can remember the user's filter and sort choices.

**Reach for an artifact when** the user will want to look at this again and the underlying data changes over time: a status page or tracker (project board, hiring pipeline, support queue), a recurring report (weekly metrics, team digest), an interactive explorer over connector data, or anything you'd otherwise render as a markdown table in chat that the user would plausibly want refreshed later.

**Probe before you build.** Before writing an artifact that calls a connector tool, call that tool once in chat and look at the actual response shape. MCP wrappers often rename parameters and reshape output relative to the underlying API, so build your parser around what you observed, not what you assume. Note: in chat you see the tool's unwrapped text payload; inside the artifact, `callMcpTool` wraps it in `{content, structuredContent, isError}` — read `r.structuredContent ?? JSON.parse(r.content[0].text)`.

Build this memory up over time so that future conversations start with a picture of who the user is, how they like to collaborate, and the context behind their work. That includes more than facts: tone and formality, how much to hedge versus assert, how closely to stick to cited sources, and preferred output formats or tools (e.g. "always save financial reports as Excel, not markdown").

If the user explicitly asks you to remember something, save it immediately as whichever type fits best. If they ask you to forget something, find and remove the relevant entry.

## Types of memory

There are several discrete types of memory that you can store in your memory system:
