# Chat-5 — Summary

Status: **closed 2026-11-11.** Handoff for the next session is
`project-logs/chat-6/CARRY-FORWARD.md`. Opened with the chat-4 carry-forward.

The owner's instruction for the whole session, given at the start: *"work from
Low → High progressively one at a time. When build is complete wrap all assets
and chat logs in our folder disk and we will shift to new chat-6."* That framed
five tasks, taken in the priority order `CURRENT-STATE.md` carries rather than
in order of difficulty — the earlier question *"are all the tasks numbered a low
medium complex tasks?"* had already established that the numbers are priority,
not effort, and this session is the proof. The second one is the largest thing
built here.

## Verification of inherited state (start of chat-5)

The carry-forward named 114 tests and one owner action. Both checked out, which
is the first time in five sessions a written push list was still accurate at the
next open. The CRLF trap was still present and still not a content change: `git
status` listed 27 files modified, `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` returned empty
for all but the real ones.

## Task 1 — D07 §14.5, governing law and venue

`e0ae738`. A counsel brief and a Phase 0 formation checklist, written so that a
lawyer is answering a specific question rather than being handed the problem.
The venue question is deliberately left **open** rather than guessed: it is a
counsel decision and the docket now says so in the place a reader will hit it
first.

## Task 2 — the independent ledger audit

`fa847a2`, record in `assets/ledger-audit-2026-11-11.md`. A fresh agent was
given the ledger, the export and the replication series and told to **falsify**
them. It found four defects, one of them critical: a rewritten chain verified
against a bundle already held, because the previous-bundle comparison checked
the slice it was given rather than the one it should have. Also a mid-chain
deletion invisible to the whole series, `INSERT OR REPLACE` defeating the
append-only triggers on the disposition table, and duplicate JSON keys reading
as two different records to two different parsers.

**One of the four was a false claim in a customer-facing document** — B01 §7 item
8 asserted a property the code did not have. That is the category of defect that
matters most in this project, because it is the one a customer could verify
against us and be right to complain.

## Task 3 — the detector ingest path

`7ea4a5c`, record in `assets/ingest-path-build-2026-11-11.md`. `POST /api/ingest`
applies the three-gate chain B02 §2 has specified since the flow map was drawn:
schema, then timestamp, then plausibility, refusing with a named reason or
holding as suspect. This narrows what D00 calls "the largest gap in this table" —
but does not close it. The schema is a demonstration schema, the endpoint has no
authentication, and no accepted reading is scored. **Building the validator did
not put a Railroad reading behind any number**, and the record says so in those
words rather than letting "ingest path built" imply otherwise.

## Task 4 — supply chain

`c401616`, record in `assets/supply-chain-build-2026-11-11.md`. Three tools:
`tools/sbom.py`, `tools/pin_requirements.py`, `tools/sign_release.py`. The
distinction this task turned on is the project's three-state discipline —
**absent, built, applied** — and all three are **built, none applied**. A
disclosed gap that is "built but not applied" is still a gap, and D09 §4.4 now
carries the state per control instead of collapsing them into one word.

## Task 5 — reviewer attribution (AD-2, part)

`2c2ee60`, record in `assets/attribution-build-2026-11-11.md`. The largest task
of the session and the one the owner explicitly delegated: asked which
attribution claim the Platform should be able to make, they answered *"unsure.
take your best approach for this build and i fully trust your experience and
expertise."*

`backend/attribution.py` adds a per-reviewer registry — append-only,
hash-chained, with `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE`/`INSERT OR REPLACE` refused —
and HMAC attestations over each disposition's `record_hash` that travel **inside
the exported record** rather than as a top-level block, because a top-level block
would fail `bundle_no_extras` and loosening that check would trade a security
property for layout. `attest()` refuses an unregistered key, a revoked key, a
key registered to a different reviewer, and a key registered under a different
certificate; `register()` refuses a key revoked anywhere in its history.

**The audit found nine defects after the suite was green, and one of them
justified the audit on its own.** The `reviewer` label in an exported
attestation was not covered by the HMAC — the message is
`axiom-attestation/v1:` plus the row hash, nothing else — so a holder of *any*
registered reviewer key could relabel another reviewer's row, re-sign the
bundle, and **both verifiers returned a pass**. That is the class of defect a
green suite cannot find, because the suite was written by the person who
believed the label was covered. The fix requires the verifier be told which
reviewer each key belongs to; the other eight are §4 of the build record.

## What the session as a whole shows

Five tasks, and **three of them ended with an audit finding something the
author's own tests could not**. Every session in this project has now had that
happen. The pattern is not that the code is careless; it is that *the person who
writes the claim writes the test that agrees with it*, and no amount of care
inside that loop breaks the loop. The standing rule — a fresh agent told to
falsify — is what has been doing the work.

The second thing worth carrying: **most of the corrections this session made were
to documents, not to code.** The registry was repeatedly called "signed" when it
is hash-chained; a customer document claimed a property the export did not have;
the revision card priced a registry as unbuilt that is now partly built. Code is
verifiable by running it. Prose is not, and prose that overstates a control is
worse than prose that undersells one.

## Commits

```
2c2ee60  Attribution: per-reviewer attestations over the disposition ledger (AD-2, part)
c401616  Build the supply-chain controls D09 §4.4 disclosed as gaps
7ea4a5c  Build the detector ingest path (B02 §2)
fa847a2  Close four audit findings; one was a false claim in a customer document
e0ae738  D07 §14.5 counsel brief and Phase 0 formation checklist
```

plus this session's transcript snapshot and handoff at close.

`project-logs/chat-6/CARRY-FORWARD.md`. Opened with the chat-4 carry-forward.

The owner's instruction for the whole session, given at the start: *"work from
Low → High progressively one at a time. When build is complete wrap all assets
and chat logs in our folder disk and we will shift to new chat-6."* That framed
five tasks, taken in the priority order `CURRENT-STATE.md` carries rather than
in order of difficulty — the earlier question *"are all the tasks numbered a low
medium complex tasks?"* had already established that the numbers are priority,
not effort, and this session is the proof. The second one is the largest thing
built here.

## Verification of inherited state (start of chat-5)

The carry-forward named 114 tests and one owner action. Both checked out, which
is the first time in five sessions a written push list was still accurate at the
next open. The CRLF trap was still present and still not a content change: `git
status` listed 27 files modified, `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` returned empty
for all but the real ones.

## Task 1 — D07 §14.5, governing law and venue

`e0ae738`. A counsel brief and a Phase 0 formation checklist, written so that a
lawyer is answering a specific question rather than being handed the problem.
The venue question is deliberately left **open** rather than guessed: it is a
counsel decision and the docket now says so in the place a reader will hit it
first.

## Task 2 — the independent ledger audit

`fa847a2`, record in `assets/ledger-audit-2026-11-11.md`. A fresh agent was
given the ledger, the export and the replication series and told to **falsify**
them. It found four defects, one of them critical: a rewritten chain verified
against a bundle already held, because the previous-bundle comparison checked
the slice it was given rather than the one it should have. Also a mid-chain
deletion invisible to the whole series, `INSERT OR REPLACE` defeating the
append-only triggers on the disposition table, and duplicate JSON keys reading
as two different records to two different parsers.

**One of the four was a false claim in a customer-facing document** — B01 §7 item
8 asserted a property the code did not have. That is the category of defect that
matters most in this project, because it is the one a customer could verify
against us and be right to complain.

## Task 3 — the detector ingest path

`7ea4a5c`, record in `assets/ingest-path-build-2026-11-11.md`. `POST /api/ingest`
applies the three-gate chain B02 §2 has specified since the flow map was drawn:
schema, then timestamp, then plausibility, refusing with a named reason or
holding as suspect. This narrows what D00 calls "the largest gap in this table" —
but does not close it. The schema is a demonstration schema, the endpoint has no
authentication, and no accepted reading is scored. **Building the validator did
not put a Railroad reading behind any number**, and the record says so in those
words rather than letting "ingest path built" imply otherwise.

## Task 4 — supply chain

`c401616`, record in `assets/supply-chain-build-2026-11-11.md`. Three tools:
`tools/sbom.py`, `tools/pin_requirements.py`, `tools/sign_release.py`. The
distinction this task turned on is the project's three-state discipline —
**absent, built, applied** — and all three are **built, none applied**. A
disclosed gap that is "built but not applied" is still a gap, and D09 §4.4 now
carries the state per control instead of collapsing them into one word.

## Task 5 — reviewer attribution (AD-2, part)

`2c2ee60`, record in `assets/attribution-build-2026-11-11.md`. The largest task
of the session and the one the owner explicitly delegated: asked which
attribution claim the Platform should be able to make, they answered *"unsure.
take your best approach for this build and i fully trust your experience and
expertise."*

`backend/attribution.py` adds a per-reviewer registry — append-only,
hash-chained, with `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE`/`INSERT OR REPLACE` refused —
and HMAC attestations over each disposition's `record_hash` that travel **inside
the exported record** rather than as a top-level block, because a top-level block
would fail `bundle_no_extras` and loosening that check would trade a security
property for layout. `attest()` refuses an unregistered key, a revoked key, a
key registered to a different reviewer, and a key registered under a different
certificate; `register()` refuses a key revoked anywhere in its history.

**The audit found nine defects after the suite was green, and one of them
justified the audit on its own.** The `reviewer` label in an exported
attestation was not covered by the HMAC — the message is
`axiom-attestation/v1:` plus the row hash, nothing else — so a holder of *any*
registered reviewer key could relabel another reviewer's row, re-sign the
bundle, and **both verifiers returned a pass**. That is the class of defect a
green suite cannot find, because the suite was written by the person who
believed the label was covered. The fix requires the verifier be told which
reviewer each key belongs to; the other eight are §4 of the build record.

## What the session as a whole shows

Five tasks, and **three of them ended with an audit finding something the
author's own tests could not**. Every session in this project has now had that
happen. The pattern is not that the code is careless; it is that *the person who
writes the claim writes the test that agrees with it*, and no amount of care
inside that loop breaks the loop. The standing rule — a fresh agent told to
falsify — is what has been doing the work.

The second thing worth carrying: **most of the corrections this session made were
to documents, not to code.** The registry was repeatedly called "signed" when it
is hash-chained; a customer document claimed a property the export did not have;
the revision card priced a registry as unbuilt that is now partly built. Code is
verifiable by running it. Prose is not, and prose that overstates a control is
worse than prose that undersells one.

## Commits

```
2c2ee60  Attribution: per-reviewer attestations over the disposition ledger (AD-2, part)
c401616  Build the supply-chain controls D09 §4.4 disclosed as gaps
7ea4a5c  Build the detector ingest path (B02 §2)
fa847a2  Close four audit findings; one was a false claim in a customer document
e0ae738  D07 §14.5 counsel brief and Phase 0 formation checklist
```

plus this session's transcript snapshot and handoff at close.

The repository is. Written push lists in this project went stale four sessions
running before chat-5, where the inherited list was accurate — which is a reason

2. This file — where chat-5 stopped and what it left waiting.

   whole build, readable cold. Regenerate with
   `node project-logs/build-history-summary.js` after any material change; do
   not hand-edit the .docx.

   the authority on docket status and the gap register.

```bash
git log --oneline -8                            # where chat-5 stopped
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD             # what is actually unpushed
git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat              # real changes only

```

this checkout. It is CRLF working-tree content against LF blobs, not content:
`git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` returns empty for those. There is no
`.gitattributes` and `core.autocrlf` is unset. Always check with
`--ignore-cr-at-eol`, stage named files only, and **never `git add -A`**.
`git status --ignore-cr-at-eol` is not a valid flag — only `git diff` has it.

pristine copy to `/tmp/mutation-attribution-snapshot` before it starts and has a
`--restore` flag. A run cut off mid-mutation leaves a file mutated; `--restore`
puts it back. Do not reach for `git checkout -- <file>` — that is how an hour of
uncommitted work was lost in an earlier session.

"Low → High progressively one at a time":

  question stays **open and labelled open**; it is a lawyer's answer, not mine.

  critical. One of the four was a **false claim in a customer-facing document**.
- **Detector ingest path** — three-gate validation at `POST /api/ingest`. Narrows
  the largest gap; does not close it.

- **Independent adversarial audit** whenever I author both an artifact and its
  checker. Use a fresh agent instructed to *falsify*, not to confirm.
- **At 150K tokens in a chat, alert the owner and roll over to a new chat** — with

  use the mutation driver's `--restore`.
- **Never `git add -A`.** Stage named files only, check with
  `--ignore-cr-at-eol`.

## Push required

`PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat`, then confirm on the commits page. The command environment
cannot reach GitHub — `git push` and `git fetch` both fail HTTP 403 from the
proxy. Until it runs, everything is durable only on this disk, and the local
`origin/main` ref is not evidence of what the remote holds.

+doc.push(H2("Stage 9 — chat-5: an audited ledger, an ingest path, three supply-chain tools, and attribution (2026-11-11)"));

+doc.push(P("Chat-5 opened with an instruction that set its shape: work the open items from low priority to high, one at a time, then wrap everything and hand off. The numbered list in CURRENT-STATE is priority-ordered rather than effort-ordered — a point the owner raised at chat-4's close — and this session is the demonstration, because the second item on the list was the largest piece of work in it. Five tasks closed."));

+doc.push(P("The first was not code at all. D07 §14.5 has carried an open venue question since the docket was drafted, and the first deliverable was a counsel brief and a Phase 0 formation checklist written so that a lawyer answers a specific question rather than being handed the problem. The venue answer stays open and labelled open, because it is a counsel decision and guessing at it in a customer document is the exact failure this project keeps finding elsewhere."));
+doc.push(H3("9.1 — The ledger audit, and a false claim in a customer document"));

+doc.push(P("A fresh agent was given the disposition ledger, the export bundle and the replication series, with the instruction to falsify rather than review. It found four defects, one critical: a rewritten chain verified against a bundle already held, because the previous-bundle comparison checked the slice it was handed rather than the slice it should have been. Two more were structural — a mid-chain deletion the whole-series walk never saw, and `INSERT OR REPLACE` defeating the append-only triggers on the disposition table, because SQLite does not fire a `BEFORE DELETE` trigger for it unless recursive triggers are on. The fourth was duplicate JSON keys, which two parsers can read as two different records."));
+  "One of the four was a customer-facing claim the code did not back",

+  "B01 §7 item 8 asserted a property the export did not have. That is the category of defect that matters most here, and not because it is technically the worst: a customer could check it against us and be right to complain. Code is verifiable by running it. Prose is not, and prose that overstates a control is worse than prose that undersells one, because the overstatement is what a regulator reads.",
+doc.push(H3("9.2 — The ingest path: narrowing the largest gap, not closing it"));

+doc.push(P("`POST /api/ingest` now applies the three-gate chain B02 §2 has specified since the flow map was drawn — schema, then timestamp, then plausibility, in that order and for stated reasons — accepting for scoring, retaining as suspect without scoring, or refusing with a named reason and logging the refusal. Twenty-four tests. This is the item D00 calls the largest gap in the register, and the record is careful about the size of the claim: the schema is a demonstration schema, the endpoint has no authentication, and no accepted reading is scored. **Building the validator did not put a Railroad reading behind any number**, and both the build record and the gap register say that in those words rather than letting \"ingest path built\" imply otherwise."));
+doc.push(H3("9.3 — The supply chain, and a distinction that had been collapsing"));

+doc.push(PB("D09 §4.4 disclosed three supply-chain gaps: SBOM, hash verification of dependency downloads, and GPG-signed releases. Three tools were built for them — `tools/sbom.py`, `tools/pin_requirements.py`, `tools/sign_release.py` — and none of them is applied. That distinction is the point of the stage. The project had been using one word for two states, and \"implemented\" had drifted to mean \"a tool exists\". The three-state discipline this pass adopted — **absent, built, applied** — is now carried per control in D09 §4.4, because a disclosed gap that is built-but-not-applied is still a gap and a reader has to be able to see which one they are looking at."));

+doc.push(P("A mistake worth recording sat in the middle of it: the pinning tool's first version pinned the hashes it had just downloaded, which records whatever the server served rather than what was verified. A pinning mechanism that trusts its own fetch is not a pinning mechanism. It was found by asking what the tool would do against a compromised mirror, not by a test."));
+doc.push(H3("9.4 — Attribution: what it closed, and the defect the audit was for"));

+doc.push(P("The owner delegated the design question — asked which attribution claim the Platform should be able to make, they answered that they were unsure and trusted the judgement. The answer built here is per-reviewer HMAC keys, an append-only hash-chained registry, and attestations that travel **inside each exported record**. The placement is a decision worth recording: a top-level attribution block would have failed the `bundle_no_extras` check added at chat-4's close, and loosening that check would have traded a security property for layout. Inside `records`, the block is covered by the bundle signature automatically, and `row_hash()` ignores it because it selects a named field list, so no existing `record_hash` changed."));

+doc.push(PB("The scheme is symmetric, and that was deliberate rather than lazy. There is no vetted curve implementation in this deployment's dependency set, and hand-rolling one in a product whose pitch includes not hand-rolling crypto would be a worse gap than a symmetric attestation whose limits are written down. Those limits are stated in the module, in D09 §4.5.5 and in the build record: the claim is *a registered key was used*, not *a person signed*, and custody is what binds one to the other. The registry itself is **hash-chained, not signed** — tamper-evident to a reader who recomputes the chain, which is weaker than authentication, and several documents had been calling it signed until this pass corrected them."));
+  "The finding that justified the audit on its own",

+  "The `reviewer` label inside an exported attestation was not covered by the HMAC. The signed message is a fixed prefix plus the row's `record_hash` — the reviewer name is not in it, so the label was decorative. A holder of **any** registered reviewer key could take a row naming somebody else, compute a perfectly valid attestation with their own key, write the other reviewer's name into the block, re-sign the bundle with the export key, and **both verifiers returned a pass**. Every test in a suite of forty-five passed anyway, because the suite was written by the person who believed the label was covered. The fix requires the verifier be told which reviewer each key belongs to; hashing the name into the message was rejected because it makes the attestation non-transferable and moves the same problem one step later.",

+doc.push(P("Eight more findings came with it: ordering checks guarded by truthiness, so deleting a field disabled the check; a check-then-write race in `attest()` between reading the registry and writing the attestation; `attest` and the export disagreeing about which registry entry is the registration after a certificate renewal, so an honest bundle failed at the recipient; malformed blocks raising `AttributeError` instead of a named failure; a docstring claiming a registry signature that does not exist; a standalone-verifier branch no test reached; and a revocation that could be undone by re-registering the same key bytes, which the mutation run exposed as dead duplicate code sitting in the wrong function. All nine are §4 of the build record and each is now a test."));

+doc.push(P("Verification for the stage: forty mutations against the three modules, forty killed, zero survived — ten of them added specifically to cover what the audit found. The suite went from 180 to 238."));

+doc.push(P("Three of the five tasks in this session ended with an audit finding something the author's own tests could not, and every session in this project has now had that happen. The pattern is not carelessness. It is that the person who writes the claim also writes the test that agrees with it, and no amount of care inside that loop breaks the loop. The standing rule — a fresh agent told to falsify — is what has been doing the work, and Stage 9's head-line finding is the clearest case yet, because it survived a green suite that had been built specifically to attack the thing it was hiding in."));

+doc.push(P("The second lesson is a document one, and it accumulated rather than arrived: most of this session's corrections were to prose, not code. The registry was repeatedly described as \"signed\" when it is hash-chained; a customer document claimed a property the export did not have; the rate card priced a registry as unbuilt that is now partly built. None of those would fail a test."));
doc.push(H1("Part III — The docket, document by document"));

# AxiomDynamics — Project Logs

This folder is the memory of the project. It exists because the work outgrew a
single conversation, and a fresh thread with no record of what was decided
rebuilds the same mistakes.

## Structure

```
project-logs/
├── README.md               this file — structure, purpose, order of authority
├── CURRENT-STATE.md        authoritative project state, updated as work lands
├── AxiomDynamics-Build-History-and-Working-Summary.docx
│                           the long-form account of the whole build (34 pp)
├── build-history-summary.js  generator for the above; re-run after a change
├── extract_transcript.py   turns a raw session .jsonl into the readable extract
├── chat-1/
│   ├── SUMMARY.md          what chat-1 did, decided, caught, and left open
│   └── CARRY-FORWARD.md    the handoff document for chat-2
├── chat-2/
│   ├── SUMMARY.md          what chat-2 did; closed 2026-11-09
│   └── CARRY-FORWARD.md    the handoff document for chat-3
├── chat-3/
│   └── SUMMARY.md          chat-3, closed 2026-11-10
├── chat-4/
│   ├── SUMMARY.md          chat-4, closed 2026-11-10
│   └── CARRY-FORWARD.md    the handoff document for chat-4
├── chat-5/
│   └── CARRY-FORWARD.md    the handoff document for chat-5
└── transcripts/            chat-2 onward, readable + raw jsonl (chat-1 is lost)
    ├── 2026-11-09-chat-2.md   readable extract
    ├── 2026-11-09-chat-3.md   readable extract
    ├── 2026-11-10-chat-4.md   readable extract
    └── raw/                the source logs, committed with each transcript
```

**Start with the build history if you are new to this project.** It is 34 pages
covering the product, every build stage and its corrections, the full docket, the
loss of chat-1's work, the internal strategy, and the open items — written to be
read cold, without the conversation it describes. Revised 2026-11-10 at chat-4's
close to carry Stage 8, the model decision, and the closure of both findings.

## Order of authority

Three layers, and they are not equal:

1. **The repository itself** — `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/` and `assets/`.
   Where a document says one thing and a summary says another, the document wins.
2. **`CURRENT-STATE.md`** — what is built, what is pushed, what is open.
3. **`chat-N/SUMMARY.md`** — conclusions drawn from the above. Useful, never
   authoritative.

If any summary in this folder contradicts a document in the docket, **the docket
governs and the summary is corrected.**

## The record, and the gap in it

`transcripts/` holds the conversation logs. **`2026-11-09-chat-2.md`,
`2026-11-09-chat-3.md`, `2026-11-10-chat-4.md` and their raw `.jsonl` files are
here** — each session is extracted and committed at its close, raw log included,
and that is the rule for every session.

**Chat-1 is lost.** It covered 2,527 turns across three raw session logs from
2026-11-08 04:24 to 2026-11-10 03:00. Chat-1 extracted readable transcripts from
them — `2026-11-08-847804b3.md`, `2026-11-08-d4e7e999.md`, `2026-11-08-2c574bc2.md`
— but wrote them into a sandbox whose storage was destroyed when the session
ended. They never reached this repository, and the raw logs went with them.

There is no copy anywhere. What survives is `chat-1/SUMMARY.md`, which is a
distillation — a judgement about what mattered, not the conversation.

**The lesson, stated where it will be read:** work that exists in one volatile
place is one failure away from not existing. From chat-2 forward every session is
extracted and committed in the same pass that produces the work, and the raw log
is committed with it.

## Standing instructions

Two, from the original build, still in force:

- **"We will keep this same concept throughout."** The physics-first framing, the
  document structure, and the numbering discipline are not to be varied between
  documents. Consistency is the product.
- **"Strictly goes in our assets folder."** Internal analysis belongs in
  `assets/`, never in `client-assets/`. Client-facing material is
  `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/` only.

A third, added 2026-11-09 after the loss described above:

- **"Drop all the entire project work directly in AxiomDynamics folder so we don't
  lose any data from sandbox."** Work is written into this repository on the first
  pass and committed in the same pass that produces it. No drafts parked anywhere
  else. The sandbox is scratch space and its storage does not survive a session;
  this repository does.

## The discipline that matters most

Chat-1's own summary records it, and the record confirms it: nearly every bad

# Transcripts

Conversation records for the project.

## What is here

| File | Turns | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| `2026-11-09-chat-2.md` | 302 (134 user, 168 assistant) | chat-2, first line to the point of extraction |
| `2026-11-09-chat-3.md` | 799 (11 user, 788 assistant) | chat-3, first line to the closing request |
| `2026-11-10-chat-4.md` | 704 (7 user, 697 assistant) | chat-4, first line to the closing request |
| `raw/2026-11-09-chat-2.jsonl` | 791 events | the unprocessed chat-2 log, 1.6 MB |
| `raw/chat-2-final.jsonl`, `raw/chat-2-close.jsonl` | — | later snapshots of the same chat-2 session |
| `raw/2026-11-10-chat-3-snapshot.jsonl` | 6,372 events | the chat-3 log at close, 26 MB, valid JSONL |
| `raw/2026-11-10-chat-4-snapshot.jsonl` | 5,667 events | the chat-4 log at close, 12 MB, valid JSONL |

The `.md` is the readable version: every user and assistant turn in order. Tool
calls are recorded inline so you can see what was run; tool *output* — command
results, file listings, screenshots — is omitted, because it is bulk without
being conversation.

The `.jsonl` in `raw/` is the source. Don't edit it. It is what the `.md` was
derived from, so if the extraction ever looks wrong, the raw file is the answer.
Commit both: an extract alone is a summary pretending to be a record.

**The chat-3 snapshot supersedes the one taken mid-session.** The earlier
`raw/2026-11-09-chat-3-snapshot.jsonl` (3,385 events, 13.2 MB) was byte-for-byte
a prefix of this one — verified by comparing the two files line by line — so it
was deleted rather than kept as a second copy that adds 13 MB and no information.
A snapshot is worth keeping only when it shows a state the final one cannot.

**This copy was re-taken at chat-3's close, which is the right time to take it.**
The session log had grown from 5,032 to 6,372 events between the first close
snapshot and the actual end — every exchange after the extraction is otherwise
lost. A transcript extracted before the last word is a transcript of the
session so far.

## What is NOT here, and cannot be

**Chat-1 — the original build conversation — is lost.**

It ran from 2026-11-08 04:24 to 2026-11-10 03:00 and covered 2,527 turns across
three raw session logs. Chat-1 did extract those into readable transcripts. They
were written into a sandbox whose storage was destroyed when the session ended,
and they never reached this repository. The raw logs they came from were in the
same place and went with them.

There is no copy. No archive, no mirror, no cache. `project-logs/chat-1/SUMMARY.md`
is the only surviving record of that conversation, and it is a distillation — a
judgement about what mattered, not the conversation itself.

**This is why it will not happen again:** every session from chat-2 forward is
extracted and committed in the same pass that produces its work, raw log included.
Nothing is left in temporary storage to be lost.

## Reproducing an extraction

The raw log lives at
`.claude/projects/session/<session-id>.jsonl` inside the session's mounted
folder. The extractor is committed at `project-logs/extract_transcript.py`:
`python3 project-logs/extract_transcript.py <source.jsonl> <out.md> <out-raw.jsonl>`.
It keeps only `type: user` and `type: assistant` events, drops sidechains and
